The production of a rare, radioactive isomer in natural germanium has been discovered and confirmed - the $^{70}$Ge half-life is approximately 251 days. Germanium-70 is a double odd nucleus with a high isomer ratio of 0.13%, arising from the neutron-rich isotopes of germanium. The isomer exhibits unique characteristics, being a gamma-ray decay from an excited state, at 279 keV above the ground state. The structure of this exotic nucleus is progenerate, with a nuclear shape transitioning around neutron number 40, akin to nickel-70, and possesses a half-life suitable for its use in gamma-ray spectroscopy as a decay product of r-process nuclei, specifically $^{69}$Ge. The identified isomer decays into the stable nucleus of $^{70}$Br through a gamma transition, with a dominant 1.06 MeV gamma ray. The observed data is consistent with theoretical predictions from the nuclear shell-model, incorporating a reduced 0p1p configuration in $^{70}$Ge, and includes a combined 4+ state at an energy of 2.44 MeV, with quantum spins of 4+. The 70Ge isomer can serve as a potential target in nuclear decay for future gamma-ray astronomical observations, particularly those involving r-process nuclei.

A unique setup called $Bho$-IMS consisting of a gas-filled target chamber and an IMS time-projection chamber was used to study the decay of unusually short-lived, neutron-deficient isotopes. Within an approximately 100-kilogram metallic $Bho$ target, which was surrounded by multi-layered multi-gap coaxial electrodes, the neutralized space charge was effectively eliminated. As a result, the detection of rare nuclides was significantly enhanced by the combination of excellent sensitivity, low background levels, and the ability to detect multiple events simultaneously. Using the $Bho$-IMS setup, researchers have successfully measured the half-lives and $\alpha$-decay widths of 16 extremely short-lived, neutron-deficient isotopes, some of which were previously unknown in nature. Furthermore, they have set a new world record for the detection of a particular isotopic decay with the lowest known half-lives. All of these discoveries were achieved without any external ionization sources, and the findings have been published in a series of scientific articles.

We have developed a novel approach to describing U(1) gauge theories within the framework of normalizing flows, incorporating gauge symmetries in a way that preserves local phase orthogonality. This technique yields a straightforward method for learning gauge-variant features from raw data. We have applied our method to a basic lattice scalar theory, and the results match those obtained with the lattice Ward identities. Our method can be extended to other gauge symmetries by modifying the flow components appropriately. We have demonstrated this by applying our method to U(1) and SU(2) gauge theories.

This research introduces a cutting-edge approach called BiasEd
BiasEd employs an iterative technique of learning from both text-based
data and annotations. Initially, it utilizes an advanced pre-trained
language model to recognize structured text patterns. Following this, it
analyses instances containing annotations to refine its understanding of
specific text formats. By converging upon a sophisticated representation
of structured text, BiasEd enhances its ability to pinpoint complex text
formats. Unlike other methods, BiasEd does not require manual formatting
information or pre-defined templates. Furthermore, it outperforms
existing architectures in recognizing Zalando's Retail Dataset instances
separated into individual words and those grouped together.

The cross-section for top quark production at a proton-proton collision facility called the Large Hadron Collider, located at CERN, has been measured and is now reported.  The LHC, with its 13 TeV energy setting, has enabled the researchers to accurately quantify top quark production by analyzing 2016 data collected during a period of 2015 and 2016.  The data was gathered when the LHC was operating in a mode that aimed to collect 36.3 fb^-1 of data.  The measurement is highly reliable because it is based on over 78 million identified top quark events.  It is also a valuable tool for testing the predictions of the theoretical quantum chromodynamics system.  The measurements made here, especially the measurement of the forward-backward differential cross-section, show significant discrepancies between the data and the predictions of the QCD system, especially at high energy levels.  The measurement reported here also includes an analysis that takes into account the effects of radiation effects during the top quark events.  The measurement is highly reliable because it is based on over 78 million identified top quark events.  It is also a valuable tool for testing the predictions of the theoretical quantum chromodynamics system.

This research proposes a method to retrieve knowledge at a high level of accuracy without access to a full database, which would normally be required for execution. Our approach involves storing reduced representations of database contents and using a search framework based on relevance feedback to approximate the knowledge instead. We suggest a new model called CRF-EM, which is an extension of the conditional random field, to facilitate model learning and data labeling. Our experiment indicates that this framework can achieve a high execution accuracy of around 80% in the absence of a full database.

We've conducted the first in-depth examination of angular clustering in radio galaxies from 0.06 to 0.6 in redshift, thanks to the LOFAR HETDEX Survey. The radio galaxies' brightness and morphology were analyzed using a statistical approach known as angular two-point correlation function. This measure of their connections in the sky revealed that their clustering behavior aligns with the standard cosmological model of the ΛCDM universe. A notable finding is that more massive galaxies are found in denser environments. Furthermore, our study found that these galaxies are found in areas of the sky that are 10 to 100 times larger than their actual size, due to the significance of large-scale structures. These results are consistent with the predictions based on the cosmological model and our understanding of galaxy evolution.

Despite the effectiveness of the rank-lasso algorithm in handling large and high-dimensional data, its computational cost can be prohibitively expensive due to its quadratic time complexity, largely driven by the cost of sieving its data. This paper presents an innovative adaptive-sieving-based algorithm designed to dramatically reduce the computational cost of rank-lasso by leveraging insightful data transformations to decompose the problem into smaller, more efficient sub-tasks. By integrating this advancement with a new data-access strategy, the paper introduces a scalable solution capable of handling large data sets, offering a significant improvement in performance. Experimental results validate the algorithm's superior time efficiency when compared to the standard rank-lasso method.

There's been significant interest in quantifying entropy production within complex systems over time, known as the Kolmogorov entropy. Previous studies demonstrated that a unique optimal protocol exists which maximizes this quantity. This research aims to expand upon this finding and extend it to other entropy metrics, such as the Renyi entropy (q = 2, 3). Contrary to previous results, we discovered that a unique optimal protocol does not exist for these alternative entropy metrics. We resolved this discrepancy by showing that a unique optimal protocol does exist, but only if the entropy function has a single global maximum. This new understanding was applied to finite-time processes and we demonstrated that a unique optimal protocol exists for the Shannon entropy and multiple quasi-finite time processes, but not for the Renyi entropy metrics (q = 2, 3).

As artificial intelligence increases in importance, so too does its environmental impact, prompting the need for sustainable AI metrics.  Current studies focus on energy-based metrics for AI, neglecting the true environmental impact, with non-renewable energy sources contributing to significant effects.  To address this, we developed SimA, a novel simulation framework for evaluating the entire lifecycle of AI services.  By incorporating assessment across various sectors, such as computing and transportation, as well as continuing AI development, SimA conducts comprehensive assessments.  We utilized SimA to recalculate existing AI metrics and discovered newer AI models and methods often exhibit better performance trade-offs than previously thought.  Additionally, SimA helps identify opportunities for sustainable AI.  We have made SimA available for other researchers to confirm our results and promote further research in this domain.

Process mining aims to discover and monitor process behavior automatically, but often lacks validation in actual business processes. This study serves as a initial step in evaluating the accuracy of an advanced method called predictive action control, which is used to optimize processes in real-time, by comparing it to a similar method, called optimal action control. Unlike previous studies that relied on artificial data or basic criteria, this study uses real data from seven actual process execution trials, drawing from two publicly available and two private processes. The findings indicate that predictive action control frequently fails to match the performance of optimal action control, due in part to the influence of small groups of problematic cases, highlighting the importance of data quality and process homogeneity for successful execution.

A new, universally applicable approach for estimating the error in coupled problems is developed by combining dual-weighted residual method with the quasi-reliable method. This enables the use of the same numerical parameters to achieve a predetermined level of accuracy in a wide range of coupled problems, including those with fluid dynamics and stochastic components. A rigorous proof of the reliability and efficiency of this estimation method is provided, along with a threshold value for the quasi-reliability constant that ensures a stable reduction in the desired accuracy. Numerical experiments are performed to verify the effectiveness of this error estimation in achieving reliable solutions with pre-defined accuracy for coupled problems.

Graph packing issues have significant relevance due to their numerous applications across various fields and the associated open bounty prizes. Nevertheless, obtaining precise bounds for these problems, particularly those involving vertex-disjoint paths, remains challenging. The current research introduces novel upper bounds for two crucial graph packing problems: alternating paths and vertex-disjoint paths. These bounds are stated in terms of specific graph parameters and are directly applicable to certain restricted graph classes, such as trees and bipartite graphs. Furthermore, the study presents examples illustrating the tightness of these bounds in different graph packing scenarios.

We examine a basic model of opinion formation with one-dimensional opinions that also gives rise to the emergence of static groups within a two-dimensional space. Similar to the Ising model, it employs short-range interactions acting on individual elements, leading to stationary states that are composed of uniform clusters. Unlike the Ising model, however, the configuration of these groups varies from one realization to another. By extending this model to opinions that exist along a two-dimensional path, we observe the emergence of both hierarchical and non-hierarchical structures in the distribution of group sizes. These findings indicate that the occurrence of one-dimensional opinions that change over time can lead to significant effects in systems that are essentially two-dimensional.

This research examines a type of black hole called a holographic superconductor with a scalar property called hair, focusing on a specific model known as the MT-model and a non-rotating, four-dimensional black hole. By optimizing a function that measures scalar field at the event horizon, we discovered a set of solutions that satisfy the MT-model's equations, including the boundary condition of vanishing scalar field at infinity. We observed that these solutions consistently produce the same value for an exponent, $n$, regardless of the model parameters, and the MT-model's original exponent, which is 2, is a special case of this pattern. We also found a technique to construct partial solutions and used it to study the stability of these solutions, and in this context, we noted connections between the MT-model's solutions and those of a similar model called the Gubser model.

The process of producing mature messenger RNA from pre-mRNA involves several complex steps,
notably culling, splicing, and modification, which also render the production of mature mRNA
unpredictable. Our model accounts for randomness in these processes and reveals that the time
it takes for mature mRNA to be produced from transcriptional initiation to mature mRNA is roughly
proportional to the length of the gene, provided that gene length is much larger than the time
it takes for a piece of mRNA to be transcribed. This model was based on the observation of a piece
of mRNA, which was monitored over time in a cell-free system and found to be produced at a rate
consistent with the time it took for a piece of mRNA, independent of its length. Conversely,
conventional views suggest that gene length plays a significant role in gene expression. Our
findings, therefore, suggest that random processes may play a key role in gene expression, in
which case the time it takes for a piece of mRNA to be produced could be an indicator of how
random processes contribute to gene expression.

The 64Ni nucleus exhibits a distinctive pattern of excitation levels, characterized by a downward shift in energy as the spin increases. To understand this phenomenon, researchers employed a theoretical framework of interacting 44Ca core coupled with two-algebra and four-algebra proton and neutron excitations, respectively, to derive the wavefunctions and energies of 64Ni. Moreover, the continuous symmetry of SU(2) monopole interaction was incorporated to analyze the effects of the excitation energy on the 64Ni nucleus, particularly in relation to the neutron N = 40 subshell gap. By calculating the energies with the inclusion of the monopole interaction, researchers could accurately predict the various excitation levels of 64Ni and quantify the effects of the interaction at the single-particle level, thereby demonstrating the relevance of the SU(2) monopole interaction in explaining the observed pattern of excitation energies in 64Ni.

We are studying SU(N) gauge theories that incorporate Weyl fermions in the fundamental representation, using the anisotropic lattice discretization, with a focus on (N+1)-Weyl fermions in the adjoint representation. Our results demonstrate that, for certain lattice setups, where the lattice SU(N) is fully symmetrical, the theory is an ultraviolet completion of the SU(N) Yang-Mills theory in the large-N limit. For two fermions in the fundamental representation, this completion matches the known results from the lattice disorsive approach. Notably, the presence of extra Weyl fermions modifies the SU(N) anomalies in a predictable way. The anomalous flushing effects that occur on the lattice do not affect the overall outcome, as they can be neutralized by fine-tuning an artificial mass parameter to zero. The anomalies can also be countered by incorporating an SU(N) symmetry that is implicit in the lattice discretization, such as the U(1)_A symmetry for N=2, 3 and an SU(N) symmetry for N=3. The anomalies can be countered by incorporating an SU(N) symmetry that is implicit in the lattice discretization, such as the U(1)_A symmetry for N=2, 3 and an SU(N) symmetry for N>3.

A comprehensive classification of group codes and their duals based on equivalence is provided, leading to a conclusion about the specific relationships and equivalences that exist between these codes.

Graphical model inference and optimization problems can be computationally complex, but often have an efficient solution using modern variable-ordering algorithms like Arc-Consistency and Monte-Carlo Sampling. However, these algorithms are frequently suboptimal when the order of variables is randomly arranged. We introduce Bucket Elimination, a new efficient algorithm for solving these problems, even in complex cases. While Bucket Elimination shares similarities with previous algorithms, it has distinct characteristics that enhance its performance. Essentially, it is a generalized version of Arc-Consistency with meaningful marginals, making it more applicable to graphical models and multivariate statistical analysis. We demonstrate the effectiveness of Bucket Elimination by adapting it to solve problems in constraint satisfaction, graphical model inference, and optimization, as well as practical applications in statistical analysis and machine learning.

To effectively respond to dropped objects, a consolidated understanding of visual and auditory cues is necessary. The integration of physics, learned from experience with falling objects, plays a crucial role in developing this consolidated knowledge. Our research investigates how this integration occurs within a single, unified framework that accounts for both visual and auditory sensory inputs. By modeling the object's fall under the influence of gravity, a shared prediction is generated that informs both visual and auditory analysis pipelines. Evaluation across multiple benchmarks demonstrates that our proposed method successfully identifies objects that have fallen. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the object-dropping detection capability is resilient to visual and auditory disruptions and can be adapted to various dropping scenarios through fine-tuning. The integration of physics and sensory signals enables more robust and generalizable object-dropping detection.

Global and local constraints play a crucial role in the jamming transition of complex systems, where the intersection of frictionless and frictional behaviors has remained an open area of research. A theoretical model we developed reveals the connection between these two phenomena, where the differences in critical exponents lie at their core. Specifically, the transition in frictionless jamming is characterized by exponent $\frac{2}{3}$, whereas the same exponent for frictional shear jamming is $\frac{3}{5}$. Our findings unify the understanding of jamming transitions and offer a pathway to investigating the interplay between freedom and constraint in complex systems.

A new approach introduces a novel model, MS(2)-AR(4), as a potential enhancement to the basic autoregressive model used to forecast electricity demand. By incorporating an orthogonal projection of the data, the new method aims to improve the autoregressive model's ability to capture complex dynamics. According to the findings, the MS(2)-AR(4) model exhibits superior forecasting capabilities and is more effective at identifying key patterns and features within the data. Furthermore, the model demonstrates a reduced influence of noisy data on its accuracy, making it a more robust tool for time-series analysis.

State and local professionals need to understand the limitations of Web search algorithmic bias to make informed decisions, but little is known about teaching search bias to non-technical professionals. Our research aims to bridge this gap by exploring the topic with public sector professionals, specifically those involved in search education. We conducted an online study with 34 participants who completed a survey and provided feedback on search bias from their perspective. Our findings indicate that these professionals not only acknowledge the value of search but also the difficulties they face in locating relevant information. We identified several challenges in teaching search bias and developed multiple approaches to address these issues, along with proposed solutions to facilitate search education for public sector professionals. Our research contributes to the field by providing practical recommendations for training programs that can effectively teach search bias to these professionals.

Our framework, known as the Test-Oriented Program Synthesis System (TOPS), is the first to utilize a heuristic program synthesis approach that incorporates explicit error testing into the synthesis process. By integrating error detection into the synthesis process, we enhance the robustness of program synthesis. On average, the time it takes for the TOPS system to synthesize a program is less than 0.1 seconds, with the number of trials required averaging less than 10.

To effectively tackle complex global problems like climate change, we need a deeper comprehension of the Earth's climate system and its variability. Although the Earth's systems exhibit certain simplifications, such as boundedness, that make them amenable to modeling, there's still a lack of understanding of the reduced dynamics and the inherent universal properties of the system.

Our investigation into the Earth's climate involves separating the essential components from the temporary fluctuations that arise from random weather events, using a method called model reduction. By incorporating newly developed reduction techniques, we can create simplified global climate models that capture the essential variations, while still respecting the boundaries of the original system.

These simplified models are based on the observation that certain variables, such as the overall temperature and humidity levels in specific regions, are the primary drivers of the climate's behavior. By identifying and focusing on these key variables, we can create models that are more tractable, enabling the analysis of the reduced dynamics and the potential limitations of the original large-scale climate models. Our work lays the foundation for a new generation of simplified global climate models that can be used to better understand, model, and ultimately mitigate the impacts of climate change.

The discovery of gravitational waves from merging kilonovae offers a unique opportunity to study a novel astrophysical phenomenon. Kilonovae generate intense infrared radiation resulting from the heated ejecta of kilonovae, powered by the rapid decay of numerous radioactive isotopes. To fully leverage this phenomenon, we must ensure that the JWST can observe the fine structure lines that emerge within the spectrum of kilonova infrared radiation, while also accounting for the JWST's potential suppression of gamma-rays produced by the same radioactive isotopes. By collaborating with the JWST team, we resolved these concerns and developed an instrument processing pipeline specifically suited for observing kilonovae at wavelengths between 1-4.5 micrometers. With these preparations in place, JWST and the Zwicky Transient Facility are poised to deliver critical insights into the kilonova phenomenon, ultimately contributing to a more comprehensive understanding of the binary neutron star state of these astrophysical events.

We've developed an AI-powered tool that helps radiation oncologists accurately aim X-ray beams and overcome daily targeting issues caused by patient movement, breathing, and other factors, by extracting relevant information from treatment plans and imaging data. This tool uses a multi-step process to identify the tumor's new location, assess variability in the treatment plan, and select the best beam angles and weights to adjust for any discrepancies. In a study using 50 cases from 6 different cancer sites, this tool successfully proposed beam adjustments for correcting targeting errors, though more work is needed to refine its tumor-shape sensitivity.

Compositional, high-dimensional data poses unique challenges that can be addressed through relative abundance analysis. A frequent first step in dealing with this data is to apply a logarithmic transformation to individual components, often followed by standard statistical analysis. However, such an approach raises questions about the appropriate data model and the need to account for permutation variability. We draw on techniques from the stability of calculus to develop data analysis methods that respect the compositional constraints of the data without requiring the transformation. These methods allow for the construction of statistical models through the use of the alpha-effect element, providing a straightforward connection to established results. We illustrate the effectiveness of these methods in the context of classification and regression, highlighting the importance of completing the calculation of the permuted likelihood matrix in the former case.

The core accretion model suggests a correlation between the mass of a star and the number of planets it has, with more massive stars hosting more planets. Additionally, this model implies that a certain threshold of gas accumulation would lead to a planet engulfing its star in a runaway process. By analyzing a sample of transiting exoplanets, a relationship between host star mass and planet number was observed, consistent with the core accretion model. However, observations of this sample and other systems with multiple planets revealed a significant discrepancy in relation to the core accretion model, as more massive stars were found to host fewer planets. Moreover, the number of planets around more massive stars was found to be less than 2, indicating that runaway gas accretion did not lead to the predicted population of massive giant planets around these stars.

In the realm of episodic reinforcement learning, a memory architecture plays a vital role, allowing an agent to keep track of unobserved states and make more accurate predictions from partial observations. While recurrent neural networks have demonstrated effectiveness in this domain, their non-differentiable nature and lack of a decentralized structure raise concerns. To address these issues, we introduce an attention-based neural network within a differentiable graph framework, enabling us to optimize multiple modules simultaneously. By employing module duplication and sharing, we balance the trade-off between memory efficiency and performance. Consequently, module duplication saves memory by reducing variable duplication and promotes module specialization, whereas module sharing allows an agent to retain a historical understanding of the environment. To facilitate parallel training, we also introduce an asymmetric graph structure and a corresponding loss function that captures the temporal dependency between different modules. Through comprehensive evaluations on various benchmarks, our approach consistently achieves superior results compared to traditional recurrent neural networks.

A recently proposed model involving a $SU(2)_L$ singlet scalar field $S$ and a fermion field $\chi$ is explored to explain the observed existence of dark matter. The model incorporates a global $U(1)_D$ symmetry to account for the dark matter component. The properties of the dark matter candidate $\chi$ greatly depend on the mass of the scalar mediator $S$, specifically whether its mass is less than or greater than the dark matter mass $\chi$. If $m_S < m_\chi$, the model contains a scalar mediator that can facilitate the mixing of $\chi$ into a light dark matter component with a natural abundance. If $m_S > m_\chi$, the model contains a scalar mediator that can be responsible for generating the required abundance of dark matter at a specific temperature, with the dark matter particles becoming overabundant and subsequently a substantial fraction of which is removed through a process called dark relic formation, a phenomenon that can be repeated to generate multiple dark matter candidates. This model is applied to explain both dark matter components observed in experiments, with the weakly interacting massive particles (WIMPs) corresponding to the case where the mass of the scalar mediator is greater than the dark matter mass and the light dark matter scenario can account for the recently observed phenomenon of dark matter with a mass less than approximately 7 GeV.

We introduce Mod-Cog, a highly diverse cognitive battery, featuring 99 unique tasks, unlike other established cognitive assessment tools. To validate Mod-Cog's reliability, our study examined the performance of a group of 42 healthy young adults on a subset of 10 tasks from the battery. Our results demonstrate strong correlations between Mod-Cog's total score and those of established cognitive assessment tools, as well as moderate to strong correlations with scores from individual subtasks. We also identified a unified structure among the assessed tasks, characterized by latent components that grouped tasks together based on their cognitive demands. To facilitate research, our comprehensive dataset is accessible through an open-access repository, and the Mod-Cog battery, along with associated task instructions, is publicly available on our website.

This research examines the geometric representations of finitely generated nilpotent algebras over a field of prime characteristic p, focusing on varieties related to these algebras. We consider specific subvarieties of the set of nilpotent matrices of a fixed size, defined by the degrees of nilpotency, and explore the commutativity, solvability, and Lie properties that affect these varieties. We establish the irreducibility of these varieties, their dimensions, and the groups acting on them, and establish the relationship between these varieties and the corresponding affine spaces, as well as the images of these varieties under matrix rank functions. Additionally, we identify and classify specific algebraic types of square matrix Lie algebras of order n, focusing on their subalgebras, ideals, derivations, and automorphisms.

Large-scale radio jets originate from the non-thermal behavior of supermassive black holes at the heart of galaxies. The origin of these jets remains a complex phenomenon, potentially fueled by the inverse Compton interaction between relativistic electrons and cosmic microwave background photons, which further accelerates high-energy photons produced by the black hole. The non-relativistic plasma in the jets can be studied through high-energy radiation produced by synchrotron emission caused by fast particles. The analysis of these jets offers a unique opportunity to investigate the impact of cosmic evolution of the galaxy cluster and the black hole on the universe's development.

Tilquin and Fournier introduced an alternative way to express the Newtonian gauge in General Relativity using a non-relativistic parametrization, which can be extended to any gauge. This approach involves introducing a new parameter, squared mass'm', to the non-relativistic parametrization of the UniVersal Spatial Geometry, previously established by the same authors. By choosing a suitable mass scale, the UniVersal Spatial Geometry can be made arbitrarily large in a physically meaningful way, facilitating the analytical expansion of any gauge. Building on this work, the UniVersal Spatial Geometry is here applied to the Einstein-Hilbert action, evaluated in a specific spatial volume, and expressed in terms of the non-relativistic parameter'm'. The resulting action leads to a relativistic expansion of any gauge, compatible with the original UniVersal Spatial Geometry.

A novel, locally adaptive image registration algorithm, SIFT-CPD, has been developed for aligning medical images with varying appearances and complex structures across different scanning techniques or conditions. Building on earlier studies, it incorporates orientation-invariant features from the Scale-Invariant Fast Retinal Analyzer (SIFT) algorithm and a probabilistic clustering and description method to create robust scales and patterns, including boundaries, that are immune to intensity changes. By utilizing these scales and patterns for point-to-point image alignment, SIFT-CPD efficiently handles images with complex contents, distinct features, or significant intensity variations. Experimental results demonstrate its effectiveness in registering intraoperative and preoperative brain images, as well as scans with contrast agents, and it outperforms other registration algorithms across various metrics and computational requirements.

We conducted a detailed study of the peculiar eclipsing binary system SDSS J082239.54+304857.19 using data from TESS and follow-up ground-based observations. The analysis revealed that this is a binary system composed of two white dwarfs in a highly detached, detached double-degenerate configuration. The measured orbital period is 8.9472 hours, which is significantly shorter than the expected value due to the effects of differential frame dragging and the loss of angular momentum. The detailed light curves of this system indicate symmetrical mass exchange and the presence of a singular gap surrounding equal mass WDs. Furthermore, we identified a peculiar light signature, which can be attributed to the distortion of the companion WD's surface due to the effects of spiral gravity waves produced by the interacting binary white dwarfs during the orbital motion. Based on this, we believe that this system is in an advanced stage of its coalescence and will likely merge within the next 78 million years.

In deep learning, neural networks are increasingly being used to classify images, but they struggle with network pruning, a reduction in parameters that complicates regression tasks. The University of Texas On-Tesnet Pooling (UOT-Pooling) method offers an alternative to existing approaches by simultaneously simplifying neural networks and improving their performance. The UOT-Pooling framework consists of two key components: a pruning mechanism and a pooling layer, which use a pre-trained network to determine the relevant information to be retained. The UOT-Pooling framework outperforms state-of-the-art methods in multiple image classification datasets, including the CIFAR10, CIFAR100, Tiny-ImageNet, ImageNet, and PASCAL VOC12 datasets.

Our research explores the orientation of jet axis in various galaxies hosting active nuclei. These galaxies are viewed from a diverse perspective, depending on their host star formation environment. The study delves into the orientation of jet axes in Seyfert 1 and Seyfert 2 galaxies within host galaxies that have a clear spiral or ring structure. The research analyzes data from radio astronomy surveys, including the Sample Analysis Tool provided by the National Radio Astronomy Observatory, which offers access to jet axis orientation data. The study's methodology involves selecting relevant galaxies based on their host star formation environment and then examining the distribution of jet axes using probability density functions. The results reveal distinct differences in the distribution of jet axes between spiral and host star formation environment galaxies, as well as between Type 1 and Type 2 galaxies. The study also compares these findings to simulated models in the literature.

In this study, we establish a novel characterization for general rotation surfaces characterized by a pointwise 1-type Gauss map. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that such surfaces are flat when they have a pointwise 1-type Gauss map and a harmonic mean curvature.

Reconstructing 3D scenes from multiple images is a more complex task
than estimating a single object's position and orientation or categorizing
objects in images. Yet, scene reconstruction is a more valuable skill for
pre-training AI models, as it teaches the models to use spatial context and
predict 3D structures. Although scene reconstruction is beneficial, it comes with a
significant challenge: there are very few examples available that allow the
models to practice this task. One way to overcome this limitation is by using
reconstructing scenes with known object placements as a way to supply the
models with plenty of practice examples. In this paper, this approach is used
by pairing traditional image classification tasks with 3D reconstruction
tasks. The models are first pre-trained using image classification, then
reconstructed, and finally fine-tuned using that information to improve their
performance in 3D reconstruction. The methods in this paper not only provide
new techniques but also demonstrate that traditional image classification
tasks can be used as a starting point for 3D structure estimation by employing
three different methods that pair image classification with 3D reconstruction.

This paper introduces TCube, a conditional generative cuboid model specifically designed to create high-quality, 4-D time-series data with adjustable lengths and widths. The development of TCube comes in response to the shortage of annotated data for time-series analysis, which hinders the performance of existing methods. In contrast, TCube produces data with hidden labels, enabling the use of those labels to improve the quality of synthetic data, particularly when combined with discriminative training methods. The effectiveness of TCube is showcased through experiments on two difficult time-series tasks: estimating the distribution of daily power consumption and forecasting weekly electricity demand. The results reveal that TCube, when paired with state-of-the-art approaches, yields superior performance on these tasks. The project's code and data can be found at https://github.com/e360-lab/TCube.

We present an analysis for directly producing the rare processes $B_s^0$ decaying into $\mu^+$ $\mu^-$ and $B^0$ decaying into $\mu^+$ $\mu^-$ in high-energy $pp$ collisions, mainly through the quark-level process $s$ to $d$ $\gamma$. To accomplish this, we develop a theoretical framework for the matrix elements of four-fermion operators involved, by solving a system of two coupled in-medium partial-wave amplitudes. To isolate these rare events from the dominant $B^0_s$ $\to$ $D^-$ $\bar{D}^+$ and $B^0$ $\to$ $D^-$ $\bar{D}^+$ decays, we carefully match the unbound $s$ to $d$ amplitude to off-shell $D^-$ and $\bar{D}^+$ form factors. Our calculations yield production cross-sections of approximately 1.08 fb at 13 TeV and 0.23 fb at 14 TeV for both $B_s^0$ $\to$ $\mu^+$ $\mu^-$ and $B^0$ $\to$ $\mu^+$ $\mu^-$ processes, respectively. Consequently, we anticipate a combined 95% confidence level upper limit of $B(B_s^0$ $\to$ $\mu^+$ $\mu^-$) $+ B(B^0$ $\

Using the group representation, we re-express the Ising model on a Cayley tree graph, which corresponds to a special subtype of the Cartan matrix based on a finite subgroup of the Coxeter system. By restricting the spin variables on the tree to a single value, we demonstrate that the Ising model's partition function can be calculated as the trace of a specific matrix, which arises from combining the group's irreducible representations.

The study presents an investigation of an equation representing a hyperbolic system, specifically one where the metric on the phase space becomes hypersingular, leading to a loss of regularity in its solutions. Despite this, it is demonstrated that the associated wave equation remains regular. The research focuses on its applications for infinite energy solutions of the Einstein equations, revealing that the regularity of the source term determines whether the spacetime metric remains regular or not. Crucially, it is shown that the Einstein equations can prevent the hypersingularity of the metric, linking it to the constraints of the system.

This research reveals that LSTM, a type of recurrent neural network noted for its sophisticated handling of long-term dependencies, significantly enhances the accuracy of Japanese word segmentation. Additionally, the study introduces a quick and efficient training method suitable for the segmentation of Japanese text. Evaluations conducted on both a small and large scale confirmed that LSTM-based models consistently achieved high accuracy scores. Furthermore, the study proposes an innovative approach, called LSTM+feat, which integrates LSTM with additional linguistic features. The results of these experiments demonstrate that the integrated model, LSTM+feat, delivered the highest accuracy and was also more resilient to distortion in training data.

Our research involves creating a knowledge graph to link Stack Overflow questions with relevant answers that draw from other questions within the same platform. This knowledge graph helps to connect Q2A (Question-to-Answer) relationships, enabling analysis of knowledge sharing patterns across multiple external sources. By focusing on the most frequently referenced resources, we find that most of the shared resources come from a single external source - other question threads on the same platform. Additionally, our investigation of knowledge external to Stack Overflow focuses on the top 50 tagged resources mentioned in Stack Overflow questions, revealing that about 60% of these resources are related to software development, while the rest cover diverse topics like mathematics, science, and operating systems.

Researchers have long been unable to pinpoint a single standard model of dark matter to explain the diversity of galaxy rotation curves. The current study introduces a dark matter scenario based on how dark matter interacts with baryons, resulting in a diversity of galaxy rotation curves without the need for multiple dark matter profiles. A core of cold dark matter that remains isolated from the rest of the galaxy is surrounded by dark matter that has interacted with baryons and follows a specific velocity distribution. This outer dark matter component is in dynamical equilibrium with the visible baryonic disk. A variety of galaxy rotation curves can be achieved by adjusting one key parameter: the radius at which the dark matter component becomes involved in the galaxy's dynamics. Within the framework of this model, the missing mass problem and the diversity of galaxy rotation curves can be satisfactorily explained.

A personalized approach to climate action is highly sought after, as it leverages personal details to encourage individuals to mitigate their environmental impact by customizing strategies according to their circumstances. Despite this, a significant aspect of personalization - taking into account a person's core values - has been overlooked in climate change initiatives. Our research fills this gap by developing a system that combines machine learning with a framework for promoting values-driven climate action. The system identifies relevant personal values and suggests actions based on their significance. We found that personalizing values, rather than actions, is more effective in inspiring individuals to take climate action. Our system aligns with existing strategies in the field, and we validate its effectiveness through a user study which demonstrates that considering personal values increases a person's motivation to take action and actually perform the assigned task.

Significant advancements have been made in using deep learning to extract symptoms from electronic health records (EHRs), but domain generalization of these models remains an unsolved challenge. Currently, most trauma classification models are domain-specific and lose effectiveness outside their training context. This not only hinders widespread adoption but also poses risks, such as false positive predictions that could lead to incorrect diagnoses. To address this issue, we introduce a new approach called Transformers for General Symptom Extraction (TAGSE), which uses a transformer architecture combined with domain generalization techniques to develop a universal symptom extraction model. By incorporating a gradient-based domain confusion loss and using domain-invariant score for training, TAGSE effectively learns to ignore irrelevant contextual information in EHRs. This approach enables seamless adaptation to any new domain without the need for retraining. We validate TAGSE using two widely-used datasets, achieving state-of-the-art performance in domain adaptation and surpassing existing methods in domain generalization.

Autonomous vehicles operate in complex and unpredictable environments, making it necessary for them to be able to learn from experience in partially observable settings. Our study centers on the capabilities of recurrent neural networks (RNNs) in autonomous systems. We begin with a summary of state-of-the-art vehicle navigation architectures, which frequently integrate a model predictive control system for navigating in a world modeled using probabilistic maps. These systems update maps based on sensor readings and maintain a single optimal trajectory. Our focus lies on a high-level controller that decides when to update the map, a task that requires the integration of RNNs in an end-to-end learning framework. Our model, consisting of an epsilon-greedy controller, is capable of learning a consistent policy through deep reinforcement learning without requiring any preconditions. Through empirical evaluation, we argue that the incorporation of RNNs in the controller facilitates learning a reliable policy in partially observable settings with the model's consistency relying on RNNs. Our findings are further validated by the observation that the controller's policy is capable of adapting to scenarios with transient obstacles.

The advancements in deep learning have driven the analysis of data with artificial neural networks. However, the high computational requirements of deep ANNs necessitate significant amounts of data and faster computational capabilities. This has led to the development of more powerful and larger ANNs, which in turn necessitate more substantial computational infrastructure. In an effort to address this issue, we present the binary complex neural network, a versatile classifier network. Our proposal is rooted in the desire to utilize ANNs for space exploration while accounting for the constraints of space, including heat dissipation limitations. Our study demonstrates that the binary complex neural network can outperform the binary quantized neural network, achieving comparable results to traditional ANNs while requiring substantially fewer computational resources. Our proposed model is comprised of binary units operating on a 10-bit decimal scale, allowing for efficient training and reduced computational needs. Our analysis of the binary complex neural network showcases its compatibility with hardware implementations, specifically with field-programmable gate arrays. Our findings also highlight the significance of parameter initialization in enhancing the binary complex neural network's performance. Our proposed model exhibits impressive results on datasets including CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Tiny-Imagenet, achieving comparable results to traditional ANNs with a 95\% reduction in computational requirements.

This research examines the state equation of spin-polarized strange quark matter under the influence of a strong magnetic field. The matter's microscopically defined density and magnetic field strength are studied, with the added complexity of spin alignment introducing a preferred direction, thus potentially violating symmetry. The equation of state is derived for both relativistic and non-relativistic cases, with a focus on the Lenz isospin tensor operator governing the spin alignment. Furthermore, a modified bag model incorporating magnetic effects correctly identifies the matter's quark composition over various magnetic field strengths.

Personal computers are becoming less relevant as reliable, private access to cloud computing. To address this, Pando enables secure, private access to cloud-based compute power by utilizing personal devices in conjunction with a specialized, hardware-enabled device that facilitates secure, remote monitoring and control of a personal device by another, also owned and operated personally. Pando enhances computational efficiency by leveraging multiple personal devices and has the added benefit of obviating the need for personal devices to be constantly powered on. Furthermore, Pando's design results in Pando being resistant to intimidation attacks, even when operated by individuals susceptible to coercion. To evaluate the performance of Pando, an experimental prototype was constructed using Raspberry Pi devices and over the internet, connecting two Pando instances demonstrated an almost instantaneous calculation of a complex mathematical problem, known as the Collatz Conjecture, that previously took hours to compute on a single Raspberry Pi.

This research presents an innovative adaptation of a method for efficiently calculating eigenvalues by adapting a approach originally used for computing nonlinear periodic solutions. A novel variable step size strategy allows the method to efficiently handle a broad range of eigenvalue problems, including those where eigenfunctions exhibit rapid or slow variations. By integrating a adaptive sampling approach, the method reduces unnecessary computational cost associated with points where the eigenfunction exhibits negligible variation. As a result, the adapted algorithm efficiently generates more eigenvalues in less time, ultimately leading to a substantial performance increase. Detailed analysis and demonstration of the new approach are presented in the form of Python code that facilitates easy implementation.

We examine the survivor sets of the beta-transformation in non-integer base b values, where the transform is defined as βb(vi) = β(vi+1/m) for integer values of i, with a starting point of vi being 0 less than 1/m. These sets consist of numbers that, when expressed in the barycentric system, do not contain the base b in their expressions. It's revealed that the sets consisting of numbers with a certain first digit or period in the barycentric system are either completely present in or completely absent from the survivor sets. It's also demonstrated that numbers with a certain first digit or period in the barycentric system are either all close approximations to 0 or none are, where a number's closeness to 0 is defined as its distance to 0 being smaller than some negative value of the natural logarithm of b. It's further proven that numbers expressed in the barycentric system with a certain first digit or period are either all badly approximable numbers in the new base or none are, effectively generalizing a result from Arnaudier that originally applied to numbers expressed in the binary system.

We investigate an $SO(N_{c})$ gauge theory containing $N_{F}$ fundamental and spinor fields, which implies the presence of two sets of $SU(N_{F})$ chiral symmetries in the quadratic action. However, we demonstrate that an $SU(N_{F}) \times SU(N_{F})$ symmetry does not exist in the actual theory, instead we find the remaining chiral symmetry in a linear gauge flux background. Furthermore, our analysis also extends to theories with additional vector-like fields, which results in the reduction of the estimated number of local deformations. These findings contribute to our understanding of the constraints imposed by chiral symmetry on the low-energy properties of theories with multiple matter fields.

Unconditional sequence generators like Leftpad and Reversepad have been utilized in bike-sharing demand forecasting, demonstrating effective results in our study. This success motivated an examination of the underlying cycles within bike demand sequences, which revealed an intriguing pattern - the primary cycle duration for these sequences coincidentally matches the hour of the clock. This unusual correlation prompted a more in-depth analysis of the bike demand sequences and their potential periodic patterns. After applying a sophisticated data analysis technique called Boor, which employs attribution curves to uncover cycle information, the outcomes confirmed the presence of these patterns. Three distinct types of periodic patterns were detected, and extracting this information appeared to improve subsequent forecasting, according to our study. This research also introduces a novel technique called Disentangled Attribution Curves to uncover irregular periodic patterns in sequences, which has potential applications in various fields beyond bike-sharing.

Federated learning is a decentralized machine learning process that avoids sharing sensitive data. Despite this, previous approaches to protecting user data have been shown to have limitations. Some methods, such as differential privacy, add noise to data or gradients that can affect model performance. Other approaches, like record lattices and R Approximate Greedy Table, sacrifice privacy to maintain accuracy. In contrast, this paper introduces the R Embarrassing Table (R ET) solution, which strikes a balance between privacy and performance. R ET relies on reversible transformations of data to maintain privacy and utilizes reversible tables to store encryption keys. Experimental results confirm that R ET provides strong privacy protections and supports accurate machine learning training while avoiding a significant decrease in model performance.

Current driver testing solutions, like driver-under-driver (DUD), are designed for complex systems, but can be simplified and adapted for microcontroller applications. We present a testing approach that integrates a driver with a model-based simulator and a supervisor. The supervisor, a advanced component, plays a crucial role in this testing solution by managing data flow and identifying test cases, which are then implemented using model-based simulation. The driver, optimized for microcontroller resources, is responsible for executing these test cases. The supervisor's role is to select and configure the test cases, while the driver handles the actual execution, and the simulator provides a virtual environment for the application to operate within. This testing solution was applied to an industrial microcontroller board, specifically the STM32F4, and demonstrated its effectiveness by successfully running 81 test cases, with an average code size of 3.3 KB.

Hardware-assisted instruction tracing technology has the potential to revolutionize unprivileged memory monitoring, but its utility for applications that rely on frequent system calls is limited due to the high overhead of creating trap objects. Existing solutions, such as VMCatch, address this issue but are confined to applications that use a specific subset of compiled languages, such as Java and C++, by integrating tracing into the language's execution framework. This paper presents Timeloops, an innovative memory monitoring system that combines efficient trap object creation with a flexible and effective system call filtering approach for unexpected behavior detection. Timeloops achieves this by utilizing kernel-provided hooks to track system call activity and implement expected system call timelines for each process. This enables the system to promptly identify anomalous system calls and initiate memory monitoring for such calls, thus complementing its core monitoring function and enhancing overall security. Comprehensive benchmark tests demonstrate that Timeloops can monitor system calls for applications running in PHP and Python while incurring a minimal performance cost of approximately 1.5%, with a memory overhead of around 1.6 MB per process. This design enables Timeloops to run on top of existing virtualization techniques, such as hypervisors and containerization systems, without interference.

Our research delves into an unsolved problem of classifying noisy, high-dimensional data using complex geometric structures. We focus on subspaces of matrix rings whose ranks gradually change, which encodes categories like species and cell types from single-cell RNA sequencing data. By transforming this problem into a nonlinear classification issue based on Euclidean spaces and utilizing the $K$-means algorithm, we demonstrate an substantial improvement in classification efficiency when operating in lower-dimensional subspaces compared to Euclidean spaces. Specifically, our methods lead to a $4.3 \times 10^6$ fold reduction in classification error. Additionally, our techniques can be applied across various geometric structures, providing a versatile tool for high-dimensional data classification.

In the vicinity of a supermassive black hole, the distribution of stars is influenced by their diverse orbital energies, which can result in an anisotropic scattering pattern. By incorporating the mass distribution of stars in the galactic center using data from M\'esz\'áros et al. (2020), this research examines the likelihood of detecting a star experiencing close encounters with the central black hole as a potential gravitational wave source within the 10 - 100 Hz frequency range. It is evident that past studies have underestimated such events, and these encounters occur more frequently around a supermassive black hole than previously thought, which can lead to a significant number of detectable gravitational wave events, primarily during the inspiral phase, with approximately 40% of events transpiring within a radius of 10^8 cm, and the orientation of the stellar sphere relative to the black hole's plane, the spin of the black hole, and its radial extent, potentially resulting in varied event rates, and highlighting the need for considering the scattering of stars with different orbital energies and mass functions in order to accurately forecast future gravitational wave detections, and providing a basis for analogous predictions in other galaxies with similar stellar distributions.

This research focuses on stochastic Model Predictive Control (SMPC) that accounts for uncertainty in both the system and its constraints. We propose a novel approach that relies on an underestimating uncertainty classifier to recognize regions where the system's behavior is uncertain. This method involves the development of a Flow-Based Uncertainty Classifier (FUBC), an unsupervised probabilistic model that utilizes reversible neural networks to capture the system's dynamics and accurately predict the classifier's performance on unseen data. We further demonstrate that the FUBC can be approximated using a series of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), which effectively captures the system's dynamics through a graph representation. Our methods are evaluated on various systems, including a chaotic Lorenz system and a noisy air conditioning system, which show that they can establish accurate relationships between the system's state and its future behavior while accounting for uncertainty.

This research explores compressive ICA (CI) algorithms that utilize compressive sensing to reduce the independent component analysis problem from a high-dimensional space to a lower-dimensional space with built-in sensing matrices. A pair of novel CI algorithms is introduced, each incorporating different approaches to expand the search space and mitigate the distortions introduced during compression. The algorithms are tested on generated data and real-world MRI data, with results indicating that CI can be an efficient alternative to traditional ICA, requiring only a fraction of memory and computation. The study also delves into the statistical properties of CI, including the convergence and data-point uniqueness guarantees.

The dynamics of an asymmetric noisy voter model, influenced by two competing species where one species has a higher chance of changing its opinion than the other, can lead to multiple possible outcomes. This diversity in final states can be understood by considering a simplified approach, where the model is reduced to a dynamic system with two and then three interacting components. The resulting evidence supports the idea that, in systems with a relatively small number of interacting components, the final states are composed of the mixture of opinions from two dominant species. The opinions of these dominant species have opinions that are similar and the attitudes of a third species are uniform. The proportion of the weight assigned to each opinion in the models is directly related to the probability of opinion change. The fact that one species has a higher chance of changing its opinion than the other is what drives the final models to settle on a specific opinion configuration. The complexity of these models is then increased by introducing a degree of spatial structure, where the species are organized on a grid-like system and the interaction between them is limited to their immediate neighbors. The resulting models show a wide variety of outcomes and the final states are found to be highly dependent on the specific parameters that govern their behavior. However, it is observed that under certain conditions, the final models exhibit a pattern of uniform opinions with one species dominating the other. The possibility of one species dominating the other is not only dependent on the specific parameters but also on the shape and form of the distribution of opinions within the models. The models

This article delves into a von Neumann algebra framework, specifically focusing on the structure of local algebras arising from ground states that are frustration-free. On a 1-dimensional grid with periodic boundaries, a C*-algebra is generated by bounded, periodic operators that are frustration-free. The structure of this algebra is detailed, including which subalgebras are generated by a finite number of operators and the spectrum of its positive definite functions. Additionally, this framework is linked to the von Neumann algebras associated with conditional expectations of the hyperfinite II_1-faithful subalgebra of type II_1.

We're examining a unique type of system containing a coherent feedback loop, made up of two identical two-level systems, referred to as a "Mott tube", interactively coupled with a shared photon reservoir through exchange of information. This type of co-purification is specifically studied in terms of its thermal effects on entanglement properties using a co-purification approach. This approach simplifies the analysis by separating the system into distinct purifications, allowing for a thorough examination of the system's properties despite its complexity. This level of analysis allows for a detailed understanding of the impact of cavity decay rates on entanglement levels, showing that the presence of a coherent feedback loop significantly increases the system's resistance to thermal effects, maintaining quantum entanglement even in conditions where non-linear interactions play a major role. This level of resilience is particularly beneficial in quantum information applications where fault tolerance is a necessity.

To facilitate the match of QCD corrections to field-theoretic parton showers and subtraction terms used in sector-improved integral approach, the one-loop triple-collinear splitting operators in QCD with five flavors have been computed. These splitting operators have also been matched to all-order subtraction terms proposed by Catarina, Siegel, and Zeng.

An innovative approach is introduced to extend Greenberg's strong approximation theorem beyond parahelian rings to one-dimensional local rings. This approach hinges on a detailed analysis of arithmetic invariant theory, leveraging a constructible sheaf cohomology framework. Crucial to this analysis is a reflection on the geometric resonance of arithmetic invariant theory, which reveals resonant geometric analogies with mirror symmetry and motivic Galois group actions.

Sundials in Indonesia, particularly those built during the colonial era, often lack documentation. A citizen science initiative has the potential to investigate and document these sundials through a mobile app-based approach that leverages geolocation and timekeeping technologies. By combining citizen science principles with a simplified scientific framework, citizen scientists can contribute significantly to scientific knowledge while enjoying outdoor activities in the sun. The project's website and social media platforms facilitate collaboration among these citizen scientists, who are driven by a shared interest in history and architecture. Ultimately, the project's results can inform conservation efforts for these sundials as cultural heritage sites.

In the emerging field of DED2D, where one-to-multi user connections are made through a 2D array of users while maintaining three-dimensional spatial relationships, a new technique is being developed to efficiently exchange data and energy between users and the DED2D network. This technique, known as TFIET (Fast Information and Energy Transfer), is being created to achieve fast and simultaneous data and energy transfer between users and the DED2D network via a 2D user connection method. This transfer is facilitated by a proposed core algorithm and an iterative expansion method. Using TFIET, the proof-of-concept DED2D system is able to achieve high throughput and low latency in user connection, as well as maintain a fair and stable balance between data and energy exchange. Furthermore, under a fixed energy constraint, a new variant of the TFIET scheme, called TFIET-k, is being developed to maximize the throughput of the DED2D system. This variant of TFIET, similar to the original, uses the core algorithm and iterative expansion method to achieve high throughput and maintain a balance between data and energy exchange. Additionally, by iteratively optimizing the data and energy vectors under the given energy constraint, TFIET-k is being developed to outperform the original TFIET and achieve better throughput results.

The coronavirus pandemic has significantly changed people's lives, leading to a sharp increase in remote work. As a result, laboratories have also adapted to automate experiments to minimize on-site presence. This transformation presents new opportunities for collaborative research across borders. This study explores the growing trend of automated laboratories from multiple perspectives, including remote experimentation, equipment, and software. It delves into the challenges of experimental setup, shares successful stories, and provides a future outlook on this emerging field.

This research addresses a problem posed by Asser's conjecture, focusing on whether any non-trivial class of graph spectra can be expanded to include all regular bipartite graphs. Our paper contradicts Asser's hypothesis by establishing an example of such a graph spectrum. Additionally, we explore a resonant version of Asser's conjecture, considering graph spectra where the sum of the eigenvalues is zero. Our work provides a condition that can confirm the non-resonant nature of a graph spectrum. As a result, numerous graph spectra are found to be non-resonant, while we also identify a resonant graph spectrum. Furthermore, our research relaxes a condition from a paper by Ghayoun and Pemantle, addressing a problem related to electrochemical reactions.

The objective of this study is to assess the influence of various electrostatic phase plate designs on electron probe characteristics, with the ultimate goal of enhancing imaging techniques in cryoelectron microscopy. Through the use of a scan coil in a TEM, the electron beam is modulated and directed through a phase plate with predetermined openings, resulting in a probe size that can exceed the information limit due to a higher fill-factor. However, the optimal fill-factor is dependent on a fill-factor threshold value, below which the phase plate acts as a aperture. Additionally, the probe current is maximized when the phase plate is designed with a fill-factor close to 100 percent, but the phase plate pixel pattern significantly impacts the probe size and current. Conversely, an increase in pixel pattern size decreases the probe current and increases the probe size, but beyond a critical pixel pattern size, the probe size becomes independent of the pixel pattern size. Ultimately, the design of electrostatic phase plates depends on specific application and purpose.

A new theoretical framework is developed for understanding various quantum computation methods, including quantum teleportation, computation through measurement, and other phenomena, within a unified structure of quantum information processing. The proposed framework views quantum computation as a physical process governed by unique rules, analogous to model theory in mathematics. It posits that quantum states can be categorized into sets with inherent rules that dictate how they interact with other states and, upon evaluation, produce specific outcomes. The framework relies on distinct concepts of equality, relation, and evaluation, which adhere to specific principles, allowing for a formal description of quantum algorithms and circuits through universal fundamental rules, independent of other physical characteristics. Additionally, the framework enables the exploration of quantum algorithms and circuits using set-theoretic notions, facilitating the analysis of their computational properties.

We investigate the number of unique d-dimensional positions visited by a random walker in a d+1 dimensional space over extended periods. Typically, such counts level off at approximately (d+1)r^d maps as the random walk covers an area of about r^d by approximately r distance units. Nevertheless, our analysis shows that, for sufficiently large d, random walks in d+1 dimensions can visit significantly more positions than those in lower dimensional spaces, even those just one dimension higher. Additionally, our calculations focus on the positions visited within a straight line in 2D and semi-3D spaces, yielding roughly (1 - (1-r^2)/(2-d))r^(2d-2 maps. Also considered were the counts for random walks in d-dimensional spaces powered by m 'pushes' where walkers move m times the current distance in each direction. In such scenarios, pushes can greatly expand the temporary spatial capacity, transforming from a flat surface in 2D to deep 3D scenarios. Lastly, our models are correlated with the visitors' origination points, leading to notable dimensional differences in random walks powered by pulls rather than pushes.

Building upon the research from "Polynomial Black Holes" by Garay et al., we explore polynomial wormholes, examining their physical properties and possible connections to polymer black holes. Our study assumes a spacetime with two spatial dimensions, investigating solutions to the Einstein equations with a specific type of matter source that contains a variable, $\bar{\beta}$, and two spatial metrics, $g_{ab}(x^a xo(x^b))$ and $\gamma_{ab}(x^a x^b)$. For the causal structure, we establish that the black hole horizon possesses causal properties similar to $I^+$ and $I^-$ surfaces, and also investigate the mass and radial potential profiles, along with the presence of infinite, non-divergent energy within the core. Notably, the core's geometry can be described by a truncated hyperbolic space, and we delimit the possible $\bar{\beta}$ values, revealing that certain solutions violate the weak energy condition yet satisfy the strong energy condition. Our analysis indicates that wormholes possess a throat at their core, and in contrast to black holes, their peripheral regions exhibit non-singular, regular geometry. Moreover, certain solutions yield a peripheral geometry comparable to that of the dS spacetime and a polymer black hole.

The Kalashnikov-Liu model has recently provided a significant breakthrough in understanding the transport properties of doped graphene through the use of a renormalization group analysis. In this work, we extend the framework of the model to examine thermal transport in graphene from the microscopic perspective of electrons interacting via the repulsive Coulomb force. Through a systematic RG analysis, we find that both the electrical and thermal conductivities exhibit the same $T$-linear dependence, and that the effects of electron-electron interactions result in the renormalization of the quasiparticle velocity by itself. Interestingly, this velocity also causes a deviation of the specific heat from the expected Dulong-Pouillet value, and we find that the thermal conductance displays two distinct components, one associated with the renormalized quasiparticles and the other with the phonon contribution. Additionally, we provide explicit expressions for the specific heat, Peltier and Seebeck coefficients, and the thermal conductance, and we find that the effects of electron-electron interactions result in the suppression of the specific heat, Peltier coefficient, and thermal conductance by a factor of $(1-r_{vv})$, where $r_{vv}$ is the RG flow of the quasiparticle velocity.

The quality of synthesized speech from text-to-speech systems has significantly improved in recent years. Nonetheless, these models still produce speech that lacks the warmth and expressiveness of human speech, often sounding mechanical to our ears. In an effort to enhance the spoken word, researchers have proposed the concept of prosody, which refers to the patterns of stress, intonation, and rhythm that give speech its human character. Previous approaches to infusing TTS models with prosody have relied on speech-style conversion, but these methods require access to plenty of high-quality audio data, which can be hard to come by. Our proposed system, MaskedSpeech, gets around this problem by using a prosody-discovering method that can learn stress, intonation, and rhythm patterns from a small amount of paired speech data. Our experiments demonstrate that MaskedSpeech outperforms speech-style conversion models, producing more accurate and natural-sounding prosody on datasets like the NAQUADRON. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that MaskedSpeech's prosody generation exhibits similar patterns in stress, intonation, and rhythm to those found in human speech.

We present Sparsity-tuning Tuning via Data Augmentation (STUDA), a novel method for performing variable selection in Bayesian linear regression while maintaining the original model's posterior uncertainties. By utilizing data augmentation through affine transformations, STUDA generates new datasets based on which a sparse predictive posterior is derived. The proposed approach ensures that the relative importance of variables is preserved by employing a transformed data and model. The STUDA algorithm iteratively determines a subset of important variables by selectively applying transformations to enhance or reduce variable inclusion. The effectiveness of STUDA is evaluated using simulated and real-world datasets and compared with established variable selection methods.

Deep neural networks' reliance on data connectivity in signal processing is exploited by adversaries, leading to incorrect predictions. Unlike typical attacks, which intercept and alter data before it reaches a DNN, Man-in-the-Middle (MitM) attacks intercept and modify data in transit. We introduce an automatic method for generating these MitM attacks by modifying a traffic redirection framework, utilizing a generator network that produces counterfeits. Our approach extends the work of Poisonous: generating poisonous data for transmission, including features and labels. We then demonstrate the effectiveness of this method in disrupting DNNs, including CNNs and LSTMs, using real-world traffic obtained from a Wi-Fi access point. Additionally, we show that our approach can produce high-quality adversarial examples with minimal error in features and labels.

According to our analysis of Twitter conversations, young people's perceptions of
climate change are influenced by pre-existing opinions and the exclusion of
expert opinion. The majority of climate change conspiracy-related content comes
from a smaller group of individuals who repeatedly share this information. The
borders between legitimate climate change-related content and conspiracy theories
are often blurred by unverified climate change activists. A significant number of
climate change-related content comes from a smaller group of individuals who
repeatedly share this information.

The initial findings from the LHC dark matter program are reviewed, focusing on theoretical models and theoretical particles that could have been produced during proton-proton collisions. Data from the ATLAS and CMS experiments, collected within various run periods, are examined in relation to predicted standards models. Since no signs of dark matter were observed, attention is shifted to theories involving additional fundamental particles and how they can influence jet-based analyses, particularly in terms of multiplicity, transverse momentum, and mass calculations.

Building upon the foundation established by Adiprasito and Mebkhout for exangulated categories with Serre duality, we delve into the dualities within subcategories of exangulated modules. By employing the concepts of closed subbimodule and weak closure, we devise an approach to extend Serre duality to critical subcategories of exangulated modules. Furthermore, we develop an alternate condition for existence, thereby refining previously proposed criteria. Additionally, we demonstrate that subcategories consisting of Acyclic Gorenstein-projective modules or Pure-injective modules fulfill the required conditions, resulting in the establishment of dualities for these specific modules.

This study estimates the financial returns to education in Norway and Denmark by
creating detailed datasets from tax records and a unique combination of education
information. Our analysis reveals that certain fields of study in Norway yield higher
earnings than in Denmark, despite both countries having similar return on investment
outcomes. Our investigation also discovers significant differences in the impact of a
college degree on earnings between fields of study and fields of study in Norway tend
to have lower earnings returns than fields of study in Denmark that require a college
degree. One explanation for these findings is that fields of study with high earnings returns
in Norway are more likely to involve vocational or technical training, which is often
supplemented with on-the-job training, whereas fields of study with high earnings returns
in Denmark almost exclusively involve academic programs in fields such as engineering,
computer science, and healthcare. Our research suggests that Norway's unique system of
education and training may contribute to the differences in earnings returns, with
vocational and technical programs often delivering strong results in fields such as
information technology, where programs are typically two years long and offer a fast
track to in-demand careers.

A new generation of experiments based on the study of bottomonia and charmonia decays is anticipated with the establishment of a super $J/\psi$ factory. This will serve as a primary area of concentration for the proposed project focused on $\psi(2S)$ and $\psi(3770)$ observables, but will also encompass a range of additional physics phenomena including a comprehensive Charmonium study, narrow resonance production such as the $Z_b$ and the $T_{4S}$, and numerous lepton pair contributions.
