A new model of ATS is proposed, incorporating the Sinclair model with a phase screen approach that accounts for underlining effects. This model efficiently accounts for atmospheric turbulence across a broad spectral range and is utilized in a straightforward calculation of an ATS's point-spread function (PSF). By minimizing the Sinclair model's contribution in the blue spectrum, an optimal ADC design is achieved. A comparison of the Sinclair model with the von K\"arm\'an model shows the former performs better than the latter for most parameters. A proposed algorithm rapidly determines an ATS's PSF given the parameters of wavelength, turbulent structure, and atmospheric conditions. This model is expectations of an ATS's behavior in a real-world atmosphere and provides valuable insights into the functioning of ADCs/ATSs.

This research introduces PILE, a ensemble method that utilizes pairwise rankings
to create a stable and robust prediction model. By combining logits from multiple
models, PILE creates a prediction that incorporates the varying outputs of the
individual models. Unlike traditional ensemble methods, PILE does not require
combine logits that have been transformed back into probabilities. Instead,
PILE uses a generalized formula to create a prediction that takes into account the
relative ranks of the logits. The core idea of PILE is that each model's prediction
is influenced by the others, allowing PILE to create a prediction that reflects
the average rank of its components. Our analyses, using both synthetic and real
data, demonstrate that PILE outperforms a range of baseline methods in creating
robust and stable predictions.

The theory of bosonic dark matter proposes that dark matter takes the form of a light, field-based manifestation of the ground state of the vacuum, traveling through space and time. To date, there has been no conclusive evidence to support or refute this theory. We investigate the potential for detecting the fluctuations caused by this potential field, known as the Poynting vector, across multiple locations within a network of sensor devices. Our analysis suggests that these fluctuations could be observable with a significant increase in statistical significance. We also explore the possibilities for improving detection capabilities by utilizing sensor arrays with varying geometries and multiple types of sensors that can leverage differing response times.

The basis pursuit problem, a linear regression with restrictions, can be further divided into two sub-problems after the matrix transformation. One problem concerns the closest orthogonal projection of an altered data matrix, and the other concerns the sparsest representation of a transformed data vector in a given subspace. A specific matrix, $\Theta$, is constructed by combining unitary matrices, $U_1$, $U_2$, and an idempotent matrix $E$. When $U_1$ and $U_2$ are randomly generated, theorems are developed to describe the statistical properties of the matrix $\Theta$. These theorems are used to derive information about the closest orthogonal projection of an altered data matrix and the sparsest representation of a transformed data vector. Combining these results with a generalized least squares estimation, a new algorithm is proposed that matches the performance of the best possible algorithms in several criteria, as proven by the same statistical properties of the matrix $\Theta$.

Lack of access to transparent and modifiable compiler backends for programmable switches hinders research in this field, necessitating an alternative approach to develop an open-source compiler backend to facilitate research, provide a comprehensive overview of current compilers, and enable compilation of arbitrary programs into switch-based designs, thereby promoting innovation in this domain.

A comparative study between the Standard Galerkin and the Streamline Gradient Galerkin methods is presented for solving the vector transport equation. These methods were further combined into a novel, two-field mixed finite element approach that incorporates the advantages of both methods. This new formulation proves to be more robust in certain situations, offering improved convergence and efficiency that surpasses the individual methods, particularly in high-contrast domains.

To address growing concerns about the ethical implications of machine learning, researchers are developing new approaches to ensure models are fair, accurate, and protect sensitive data. The integration of fairness metrics, federated learning, and differential privacy represents a significant advancement in this area, but efficient optimization of such complex frameworks remains an unresolved issue. The current state of tools fails to effectively bridge the gaps between statistical fairness metrics, numerical optimization techniques, and data distribution methods. To resolve this, we developed Sypder - an open-source library combining established and innovative techniques to provide a unified framework for optimizing fairness and data transmission in federated learning under differential privacy. The library's capabilities include scalable optimization frameworks, a comprehensive compiler that translates fairness metrics into executable code, and a data abstraction model that facilitates use with popular machine learning libraries, and is shown to be compatible with established models. We demonstrate the effectiveness of Sypder through experiments on both synthetic and real-world data, achieving fair models that meet stringent privacy requirements while maintaining performance compared to models trained on unprotected data. The Sypder library is accessible at https://sypder.github.io.

A comprehensive LHCb, CMS, and ATLAS search for the $B_c^+$ being produced in proton-proton collisions has been conducted to identify its excited states. The examination involved analyzing 12 fb$^{-1}$ worth of data collected at 13 TeV. The researchers looked at specific decay patterns of the $B_c^+$ to know when its various excited states are formed and what particles they are composed of. Based on the analysis, two excited states of the $B_c^+$ were identified and are composed of a $B_c^0$ and radiation. The identified states have since been recognized by the CERN particle table and include the $B_c^*(2S)$ and $B_c_1(2^+; 2S)$. The examination also provided a minimum lifetime limit of 0.70 pb for the $B_c^*$ state and 0.50 pb for the $B_c_1$ state. The discovered $B_c^*$ and $B_c_1$ states have since been recognized by the CERN particle table and match theoretical predictions made in the context of the mass-charming quark model.

Our analysis reveals that conventional continuous-stage Runge-Kutta methods actually correspond to implicit Dirk-type methods when applied to Hamiltonian problems, and we subsequently examine their explicit variants.

Deep Neural Networks such as Convolutional Neural Networks and Recurrent Neural Networks exhibit slow training times due to the high computation required for backpropagation. Previous research proposed distributing the computation across a cluster by dividing it into an ensemble of identical Neural Networks. Each network in the ensemble calculates a partial derivative, then the ensemble calculates a gradient through a collector module, ultimately learning a single common parameter for all networks. Our study starts by analyzing the shortcomings of this distributed training approach. Then, we introduce an efficient training method called local critic training, where each network calculates its local gradient and corresponding update. Our novel gradient estimator accurately calculates this gradient across a cluster. By combining local training with our gradient estimator, NRT (Neural Network ensemble with local gradient estimator), the efficiency of training deep Neural Networks is greatly increased. Our analysis also demonstrates that with minor adjustments, multiple gradients can be calculated using our gradient estimator, enabling the simultaneous training of multiple Convolutional Neural Networks.

In our investigation of a chaotic waterwheel known as the Swirling Pot, we discovered that its unusual basin structure, dubbed a Wada basin, collapses when subjected to extremely low levels of dissipation. This finding came as a surprise, as dissipation is generally considered to enhance a system's stability. By analyzing the system's topological properties, we found that the source of its instability lies in a singular boundary point where the system's structure converges. When we applied a novel theoretical framework, it indicated that the system's ability to withstand errors is a rare occurrence. To verify this, we conducted an experiment that successfully transformed the system into a perfect predictor of its outcomes.

In light of recent research highlighting a muon g-2 anomaly, we examine how a future lepton collider can explore related new physics. Our findings are based on a muon g-2 measurement at a muon collider, leveraging muon beam polarization to detect deviations in the muon's magnetic moment. Our analysis suggests that a 1.5 TeV muon collider with a 2 ab^-1 integrated luminosity, or a 32 GeV muon collider with a 5 ab^-1 integrated luminosity, has the capability to cover the majority of the relevant new physics parameter space. However, these options come with the drawback of lower event rates compared to a typical lepton collider. To mitigate this, we propose an optimized production mode: a 32 GeV muon collider operating in a 2-beam isobar configuration with a high luminosity of 10^36 cm^2 s to collect 5 ab^-1 of data in a relatively short 5.6 fermi year.

This paper introduces the Hierarchical Attention Network (HAN), a hierarchical attention mechanism that focuses on multiple temporal steps and incorporates context information in each step. HAN is designed to solve the problem of action recognition in unsupervised and semi-supervised settings. At each step of the attention process, Context Information is used to guide the selection of subsequent steps, in contrast to purely sequential approaches. To construct the context information, HAN employs a Context Network that utilizes all previous steps. Additionally, HAN incorporates a Context Information propagation system to resolve time inconsistencies between attention and spatial temporal analysis. Experiments have demonstrated that HAN achieves impressive performance that surpasses existing methods on widely-used datasets, specifically UCF101-90% and HMDB51.

Using the anti-de Sitter / CFT correspondence, we've been able to simulate black hole scalar field scattering. Our initial investigation involved creating black holes with high energy, and then subjecting them to a scalar field via a boundary perturbation. This boundary perturbation represented the equivalent impact of a plane wave in physical terms. Our study focused on two types of black holes: those near the absolute minimum and those at the absolute minimum. Interestingly, the resulting outcomes exhibited significant differences. For near-extremal black holes, we observed a steady emission of scalars, accompanied by a rotation of the black hole's spin. Conversely, the extreme black holes displayed a more intriguing behavior, leading to the formation of a quasi-stationary scalar field. Our analysis indicated the presence of a single rotational mode and a series of gravitational modes. Notably, the frequency of these gravitational modes mirrored that of the original black hole, despite the changes. Our study was also able to achieve a theoretical approximation of the final state using holographic gauge theory descriptions.

The exploration of star formation across various galaxies allows us to examine the process of life creation in the universe.  A comprehensive classification system for star formation in galaxies has been developed, considering both vibrant regions and less-active ones. Research into the more extraordinary types, like those with tandem gamma-ray burst hosts and massive star-forming galaxies at great distances, is particularly intriguing. At this point, only a handful of examples exist for each of these exceptional classes. To further the understanding of star formation, it is necessary to collect more data and construct probabilistic models using existing information. These models can then be utilized to make accurate predictions about the characteristics of newly discovered galaxies.

Computing entropy properties for disparate data represents a prevalent issue. The issue arises because some probability distributions are too complex to accurately calculate directly. By utilizing the quantized normalized permutation entropy, researchers have developed an alternative method to estimate entropy properties in such cases. The quantized normalized permutation entropy strikes a balance between precision and simplicity, enabling the calculation of entropy properties for even the most intricate data. The method's effectiveness was tested on financial time series and the study found it to be robust against various issues that can affect its accuracy, including the impact of distinct data patterns and noise levels. Furthermore, the method was able to identify distinctive patterns in the entropy properties of different data sets, highlighting the method's utility in characterizing complex data. The study also discovered that the entropy properties of certain data sets exhibit time-dependent changes over time, while others exhibit consistent patterns throughout their duration. The investigation further revealed that the time-dependent behavior of these properties is correlated with the time-dependent behavior of specific financial indicators, suggesting that the method has the potential to improve our understanding of financial markets and predict future market trends.

A dynamic Borel measure represents a non-negative Borel function on a space related to a semiconductor manufacturing system. This paper examines Borel measures in two key aspects: first, it identifies a subset of measures describing system states, and second, it explores a broader subset of measures describing system change over time (or equivalently, system evolution). A notable connection exists between these measures of state and measures of change: measures of state essentially capture static aspects, while measures of evolution embed dynamics. Demonstrating that a given measure describes system states or evolution involves a two-step process: verifying a certain condition derived from Kolmogorov's consistency theorem, and then applying an algebraic and topological structure identified in a previous paper. This validation can be seen as describing the system's behavior through a non-additive probability theory called "borned measures," where a partial order plays a crucial role in interpreting measurement outcomes. This paper also discusses how borned measures can represent additive probabilities, shows that a substantial set of measures describing evolution are essentially periodic, and further examines measures describing systems with cyclic behavior.

To achieve more accurate and efficient threat detection on resource-constrained devices, we have developed NBcoded, an innovative tool that combines lightweight neural networks and binary coding techniques. NBcoded utilizes binary coding, specifically binary weight neural networks and binary encoding of activation functions, to create compact and readable models that can be easily understood and customized. Utilizing this approach, NBcoded extracts feature vectors from input data and encodes them into binary strings that can be classified into positive or negative categories, effectively addressing the limitations of one-bit activation functions that hinder previous methods. NBcoded utilizes an optimization algorithm based on gradient descent to refine its approach and maintains the accuracy of its core learning process while reducing complexity, and has been implemented in a versatile command-line tool that facilitates model training, testing, and sharing on a variety of platforms, including Google Collab and Jupyter Notebooks.

The metamorphic growth rate of a group $G$ is defined as the limit superior of the sequence $|G^n|/|G^m| - 1$, where $n$ and $m$ are positive integers. It's known that this growth rate is invariant under automorphisms of $G$. We explore the metamorphic growth rates of metabelian groups, which have abelianization, and find that these groups can be classified into three main categories based on their properties: those that are finitely generated but not finitely presented; those that are finitely presented but not torsion-free; and those that are torsion-free. We've identified the possible ranges of their growth rates and determined the lower and upper bounds of growth rates for specific types of metabelian groups, such as those presented by linear equations and torsion-free solvable groups.

In recent years, researchers have made significant progress in building artificial cells using synthetic components. We propose an automated approach that generates artificial cell behaviors by producing sequences of cell movements. Our method aims to differentiate between biological movements and non-biological object movements by continuously reassembling cells. To achieve this, we introduce a new transformation called cell migration, which allows us and others to create artificial cells using automated cell migration. We then tested this idea in a simulation environment where we observed the movement of our artificial cells and were able to extract a code representation of this movement. Our results show that this representation can be generalized across different sizes and shapes of artificial cells. We also found that this representation can be used to generate artificial cell movements that are distinct from the movement of non-biological objects. To verify the efficacy of our approach, we conducted a user study where we examined the effect of our artificial cells on two tasks and discovered that the presence of our synthetic cells improved task performance compared to having just the non-biological object or nothing at all.

This work explores the application of hybrid approaches that combine quantum computing and classical methods for integer linear programming, specifically focusing on the partitioning of multi-terminal edges in power networks. By merging the efficient classical solutions of complex optimization problems with the precise quantum approaches to sub-problems, this research introduces four hybrid methodologies that yield substantial computational gains. Furthermore, the study introduces a quantum-based partitioning technique that leverages edge colorization and utilizes the minimum spanning tree principle to generate colored terminus partitions. To test and evaluate these hybrid methods, the study employs a standard power network benchmark modified to mimic the characteristics of modern energy transmission systems. The results demonstrate that these hybrid approaches not only reduce computational complexity but also result in faster practical solution times, even when considering the current limitations of quantum computing.

The acceleration model, a fundamental physics concept, is tested with objects that experience drag forces. Measurements of noise and unsteady drag forces using high-speed cameras lead to the development of a new modeling approach. This modeling approach accounts for complex noise and unsteady drag effects, contradicting simpler drag models that have been validated in previous experiments. Additionally, the results reveal that the noise and unsteady drag components are comparable to steady drag forces in strength, suggesting that they play a significant role in falling object accelerations. These findings have significant implications for physics teaching and can guide research in fluid dynamics and experimental methods.

A cutting-edge collider such as the Future e+e- collider, capable of producing a vast array of supersymmetric particles, presents an ideal testing ground for a broad range of supersymmetry models. Given the supersymmetric particles' short lifespans, the detector's precise localization capabilities become redundant, and the risk of tagging the supersymmetric particles is correspondingly minimized. In this investigation, we examine the supersymmetry models characterized by the mass range of 100 GeV to 3 TeV for certain particles and assume the suspension of supersymmetry models characterized by the supersymmetric particles' rest masses less than 100 GeV. We then investigate the supersymmetry models characterized by the squarks and gluinos' mass range of 1 to 3 TeV, tagged by their creation during the two-body annihilation of gauge bosons or the combination of s-quarks. We focus on the prospects of detecting the supersymmetry models characterized by the suspension of SUSY models and minimal supersymmetry, plateaus, and compressed supersymmetry, as these scenarios offer optimal conditions for the creation of the supersymmetric particles and the suppression of the reverse reactions. We also find that the mass difference between the supersymmetric particles and the standard model particles could be determined with a high degree of precision by concentrating on specific production processes and examining the supersymmetric particles' decay patterns.

We designed and tested a novel single-device system that enhances single-photon performance by utilizing a tapered microfiber in a single-photon source. The design combines a linearly tapered section with exponential tapering to increase its single-photon efficiency and transition speed. The device was examined using both experimental and theoretical methods, showing high single-photon efficiency and rapid switching times. The efficiency improvement offers enhanced coherence for multi-mode interferometers and the speed enables the generation of multiple single photons per optical cycle. This advances single-photon technology, potentially expediting the development of leaky-mode single-photon sources and photonic topological insulators.

The soft potential model, tailored to HfO$_2$ and similar materials, incorporates a broad ensemble of potencial energies corresponding to longitudinal and transverse sound modes. This model effectively captures the anomalous skewness in the frequency-dependent damping of longitudinal sound waves in HfO$_2$, which cannot be explained by a Sharir-like mechanism. Furthermore, the model reveals that at low frequencies, the damping of longitudinal sound waves in these materials exhibits a frequency-independent behavior. Conversely, the damping of transverse sound waves follows a normal frequency-dependent behavior. A modified elastic constant is also introduced, which is shown to be influenced by the parameters of the broad ensemble. This model may have a broad range of applications in the theoretical analysis of dielectric properties and other characteristics of these materials.

We introduce a novel, semi-numerical approach to computing renormalizable particle interactions, which combines analytical and numerical techniques. By breaking down processes into simpler components and representing their corresponding amplitudes with polynomial functions, our method leverages recent advancements in modern Riemannian geometry to constrain the polynomial space. The constraints are then translated into a solvable mathematical problem, and the resulting equations are analyzed using numerical methods. The semi-numerical approach yields results similar to those from full numerical lattice simulations but achieves these computations much more quickly, at a significantly reduced cost.

A specific classification of quantum states, known as eigenchannels, has great implications for understanding quantum transport and radiation phenomena. These eigenchannels are uniquely determined by the eigenvalues of a transfer matrix, which in turn can be derived from calculating the steady-state intensity distribution of waves in a homogeneous and isotropic medium following a brief pulse initiation. This steady-state intensity distribution is essentially the coherent sum of plane waves, each representing a specific propagation distance, and the coefficient of each wave, known as a "fingerprint" in the study, varies depending on the medium's properties. The study finds that the fingerprints alone, regardless of the complexity of the medium, can precisely identify its properties and therefore facilitate the identification of different materials. Notably, the technique requires minimal information about the pulse. Following the validation of the proposed method using numerical simulations of scattering experiments, the study successfully applies it to analyze data from real-world experiments involving glass and Teflon materials. The study also presents a theoretical explanation for the phenomenon.

Despite expectations, the presence of a galactic bar at the center of the Milky Way remains controversial. To clarify this, researchers conducted a thorough investigation into the variable K-band nugget population within three degrees of the galactic center using data from the VISTA Galactics survey. After accounting for extinction and proper motion, a clear spiral structure in the K-band nugget distribution was found extending from the center of the galaxy out to approximately three degrees. Furthermore, a distinct nugget disk was discovered at a radius of around 0.5 degrees, consistent with a bar structure. Additionally, evidence suggests that the bar is most likely perpendicular to the plane of the galaxy. Based on these findings, researchers concluded that the center of the galaxy contains a bar structure consistent with a flat extent of approximately three degrees.

Multi-modal optimization tasks are commonly associated with with the goal of finding diverse coeﬃcients that enable multiple objective functions to be simultaneously satisfied. In contrast, multi-objective optimization eﬀorts tend to yield coeﬃcient sets with varying ﬁtness levels. By treating each modal as a separate objective, we propose a novel multimodal optimization strategy that employs a diﬀerentiate-to-the-mean penalty (DTM penalty). This DTM penalty shares similarities with the diﬀerentiate-to-the-mean penalty used in multi-objective optimization. Our research ﬁndings demonstrate that the penalty's eﬃcacy is dependent on the modality distribution and that it exhibits stress and Pareto eﬀectiveness under specified conditions. Furthermore, we outline the potential for our multimodal optimization method to outperform other multi-modal optimization approaches and point out an interesting connection between our work and the multi-objective optimization framework.

Research on stable matchings has been diverse, spanning over five decades, 
and two distinct approaches exist for determining stable matchings: 
general valuations and specific constraint problems. Initially, the focus 
was on finding stable matchings for general valuations, but more recently, 
the focus has been on problems with specific constraints. These constraint 
problems often involve finding stable matchings with specific limitations 
such as limited choice or distinct groups. In this paper, we investigate 
the problem of finding stable matchings when agent valuations are binary and 
either sum or maximum values. We introduce new concepts: majority stable 
matchings and binary stable matchings. A matching is considered majority 
stable if no pair has two alternatives that would prefer each other over their 
current matches. A matching is considered binary stable if no pair has two 
alternatives that would prefer each other over their current matches and both 
options being chosen. We can find a majority stable matching in near-linear 
time: specifically, we can find a majority stable matching in O(log^2 n)/poly(
log n) rounds of O(log n)/poly(log n) communication. We can also find a 
binary stable matching in a distributed manner with specific complexities: 
specifically, we can find a binary stable matching in O(log^2 n)/poly(log n) 
rounds of O(log n)/poly(log n) communication. We also introduce two new

Recent studies have focused on valley Hall effect in nonuniform strained two-dimensional semiconductors, typically made from heterojunctions of hexagonal graphene/hexagonal h-BN and InAs/GaSb. These investigations, however, lack a comprehensive framework that incorporates both strain variations and valley interference. Our model, founded on a combination of the Huckel method and the Kane-Assad equations, has enabled us to calculate transport properties of valley Hall currents in strained channels. Our analysis reveals that strain fluctuations have a significant impact on valley Hall currents and can mask their Hall characteristics. Moreover, valley interference Valley Hall's signature is only visible in the subband contributions of valley Hall currents, not in the valley Hall itself. Our theories are applicable to valley Hall experiments, inquiring about valley Hall currents in strained channels and validating valley interference.

We establish that for any action of a countable group G on a countable set X, and a cloud C consisting of nontrivial stabilizers, it is possible to create a metric space by incorporating the fibers of C into X, such that the center of this space lies within a countable subset of its diameter.

A curved faceted antenna designed for deep space communications has a 6-layer parabolic antenna with 7 curved and 6 faceted facets, operating at 8.4 GHz with a matched bandwidth of 1.3 GHz (816-857 GHz), featuring a 3.1/(λ) gain, 0.55/(λ) cross-polarization rejection ratio, 0.46/(λ) sidelobe level, and a 19.9/(λ) spotbeam to mainbeam ratio. The antenna has 33% increase in gain and 20dB increase in sidelobe level compared to a 5-layer design, with a 2.5/(λ) gain and 15dB sidelobe level from a 6-layer faceted design at 8.4 GHz, providing a 100% matched bandwidth. This 6-layer design has a 22 degree half-power beamwidth, 9.2 degree cross-polarization beamwidth, and a 0.87 number gain accuracy within the matched bandwidth. The curved faceted design reduces weight and increases stiffness with a 0.06 kW/l peak power density and a 0.06 kW/ln area ratio peak power density.

To enhance the precise readout of quantum circuits, researchers have employed machine learning in conjunction with reinforcement learning. This technique involves using a decoder designed for conventional channel reading, but with a twist - it's been modified to optimize its operations on imprecise readings of quantum states, thereby simulating the behavior of conventional channels. This approach offers a straightforward way to enhance the reading process of quantum circuits, particularly in cases where the circuits are prone to errors that can be corrected. Notably, this method has proven to be particularly effective in decoding the surface code up to distance 10 on any single qubit, with comparable results for codes with longer distances. This breakthrough suggests that reinforcement learning holds great promise for improving the decoding of quantum error correction strategies.

In quantum state measurement, multiple data samples can be processed in a single analysis to achieve optimal results, something that's not possible in real-time data analysis.  We've developed a new technique called quantum jump metrology that leverages post-processing of non-real-time data to precision limit optimization.  This approach uses a simplified simulation model to demonstrate its effectiveness and efficiency for complex systems, even when numerous data samples are required.  We're applying this method to optical lattices and atomic clocks, and it offers enhanced precision over traditional methods.  The quantum jump metrology technique has widespread applicability and can be applied to various quantum systems where real-time data analysis is challenging.

A study on the production of hadrons in Au+Au collisions has been conducted across a full range of momentum findings, from direct measurements to calculated estimates, in a collision energy of 200 GeV per nucleon pair.  The measured hadron yields are examined in relation to their calculated counterparts from a quantum computer simulation.  Additionally, the study examines how certain hadron creation processes are affected by the momentum of their parent quarks.  It discovers that, as a quark's momentum decreases, the overall yield of hadrons increases.  This phenomenon is consistent with previous findings from smaller collision energies.  Examination also reveals that certain hadron creation processes involving a quark and an antiquark contribute more significantly to lower-momentum quarks.  These findings support the idea that lower-momentum quarks are involved in more numerous and colder quark-gluon interactions.

Researchers have devised a method to use quantum computers that combine digital and analog components to simulate complex many-body systems, even when digital methods face scalability limitations. This combined approach allows for an exact simulation of the Fermi-Hubbard model using analog quantum circuits to handle the interactions and digital circuits for the linear part of the Hamiltonian. By further developing this concept, scientists have leveraged the analog circuits' ability to smoothly vary the interaction strength to discover novel features of the model. Without this adaptation, achieving a precise control over interaction strengths, especially for complex systems, would be extremely difficult. This breakthrough makes it possible to explore the quantum crossover from the Fermi-liquid to the spin-fluid phase, which also enables the discovery of critical properties of the model. What's more, the analog component allows for the simulation of random variations in the system, leading to a phase diagram with multiple coexisting phases when this randomness reaches a certain threshold. This innovative method not only facilitates the simulation of the Fermi-Hubbard model, but it also opens up new possibilities for the computation of other many-body systems as well.

Automatic feature creation is a key benefit of AutoML and deep learning systems. Previous approaches involved supervised feature reduction and learning, but struggled with high computational costs. To address these issues, a new algorithm called Bonsai is proposed, which uses unsupervised learning to create feature representations. By integrating a novel attention mechanism and a hierarchical attention network, Bonsai achieves both efficient computation and improved performance. As a result, Bonsai outperforms existing methods in various numerical and categorical prediction tasks, and its computations are significantly faster. The algorithm uses Bonsai trees to combine attention mechanisms and learning, resembling decision trees but with numerical parameters. During training, Bonsai adjusts these parameters to maximize prediction accuracy, utilizing gradient-based optimization and feature attention to refine its results. Additionally, Bonsai utilizes feature attention to eliminate unnecessary features from the original feature set, resulting in reduced dimensionality and faster computation. Due to its reliance on numerical Bonsai tree parameters, Bonsai can be efficiently trained on GPUs.

A novel genetic algorithm enhances the resolution and contrast of light passing through scattering media by utilizing different weights for mutations. This adaptive approach optimizes the weight values iteratively using a directed correlation metric that minimizes noise and maximizes image clarity. A comparative study demonstrates that this weighted-mutation technique consistently yields higher-quality images and more efficient optimization compared to traditional genetic algorithm methods. Furthermore, the found optimal weight values exhibit recurrent and near-periodic patterns, which are independent of the specific image being optimized, as validated by extensive simulations. This weight-value database can be employed as a precursor for future algorithms that integrate additional optimization techniques within the genetic algorithm framework.

We investigated multiple policy learning techniques using value function estimates derived from a biased sampling approach. This approach draws a testing sample to enhance training, offering a more efficient path than sampling a matching distribution. The method provides value function estimates on a held-out dataset while remaining dependent on a weighted subset of the training data. Our findings reveal that efficient VFEs can often approximate the policy's optimal values with high accuracy when dealing with a large testing sample. However, a relatively small testing sample may lead the VFE to severely overestimate the policy's values. To address this issue, we developed two new improvements: multi-sample averaging, which calculates VFEs from multiple testing samples and significantly mitigates overestimation; and a counterfactual prediction strategy, which predicts VFEs for a policy based on a collection of existing datasets. Our empirical results confirm that these innovations produce reliable VFEs with high accuracy. Moreover, we discovered that efficient VFEs can learn to prioritize sensitive data while remaining relatively insensitive to data manipulations, highlighting the potential of this approach to improve data security.

This research investigates the properties of a monolithic small collection-electrode CMOS sensor featuring a p-sensor layer and an n-bulk sensor, fabricated using a CMOS process incorporating a high-resistivity epitaxial collection layer. The sensor, consisting of sensors with varying sensor layer thicknesses of 50 $\mu$m and 300 $\mu$m, was tested to examine its characteristics in relation to radiation. Charge collection properties, influenced by deep defects and space charge, were 3D-simulated to furnish design parameters for the sensor design. Furthermore, the sensor was tested under x-ray and beta radiation, with the aim of exploring its operation in a monolithic active pixel sensor mode.

The analysis of zonal images in ground-based exoplanet detection is complicated by the non-uniformity of these images. To rectify this issue, a new algorithm called PCA-RLT is suggested, which utilizes a regional transformation based on principal components to normalize the images. This approach draws on the standard RLT (Rice-Lancaster) technique, which is applied to each zone of the field of view. By comparing it to the TPS-RLT method, the results show that PCA-RLT offers superior performance in restoring the point spread function (PSF) of the system, even when the images are irregular. Consequently, this technique enhances the signal-to-noise ratio and signal-to-noise ratio for exoplanets of various sizes.

This study introduces a conditional distance-dependent stochastic volatility model with a non-normal distribution, capable of handling negative interest rates. By combining the non-normality approach with a dynamic conditional distance, the model effectively captures the rapid time changes in volatility and skewness/leptokurtosis. A discrete-time continuous-time approximation method is employed to estimate the model, which enables the calculation of critical risk management measures. Notably, the model can be expanded to a multi-asset framework, offering a potential solution for modeling complex financial time-series data.

The DUNE Near Detector is designed to track neutron and ionization-level interactions at a 1.5-meter depth within a 40-ton liquid argon detector at the crossroads of three neutrino oscillation experiments. Situated near the end of a 70-meter-long beam tube, the detector is optimized to monitor a substantial proportion of the neutrino events produced by a sub-GeV neutrino oscillator at the heart of the three experiments. As a consequence of its comprehensive design, the detector is well-suited for not only its primary role but also potentially to detect neutrinos produced directly by a high-energy proton driver at the heart of the three experiments, thereby widening its scope to include neutrino energies in the range of 10-100 MeV. By doing so, the detector may be adapted to search for previously overlooked signs such as sterile neutrinos or non-standard interactions in addition to its core purpose. In this study, we simulate and assess the detectable sterile neutrino and non-standard interaction signatures across various models and scales in the range of 10-100 MeV using the DUNE Near Detector configuration.

This research introduces a set of enhanced, cluster-specific estimators for cluster-specific and cluster-adjusted analyses. The newly developed estimators exhibit superior performance in small sample scenarios, surpassing previously established methods. Specifically, our work evaluates the performance of these estimators through simulations under diverse within-cluster and between-cluster data relationships. The simulation results demonstrate that the newly proposed estimators outperform traditional approaches in terms of precision and computational efficiency, particularly for smaller cluster sizes. Consequently, these estimators are poised to boost the reliability and efficiency of conventional cluster-based analysis techniques, ultimately leading to more accurate inferences. The proposed estimators are readily available for public use through the implementation of a publicly accessible R package, clusterRobust.

A novel integration approach, the multiple-time-step algorithm (MTSA), has been developed to optimize the computation of fluid particle interactions in incompressible flow simulations by dividing the calculation process into sequential stages.  Depending on each particle's local time-step size, MTSA assigns them to respective stages where their positions and velocities are updated, and then, the pressures in the surrounding fluid grid are calculated using a specific method.  After that, a different stage is handled using another pressure-based method that uses a predictor-mesh approach to refine the fluid velocities and dwell in that stage until a predetermined criterion is met, leading to fourth-order accuracy for the entire algorithm.  Furthermore, our implementation also took into account the fluid grid's convective transport by introducing an additional stage, enabling the solution to approach a more direct fourth-order accurate representation.  Through detailed analysis and numerical tests, our multiple-time-step algorithm has demonstrated its potential to significantly lower computational costs by reducing the complexity of fluid particle interactions and can serve as a highly efficient alternative to traditional fluid-particle coupling methods.

The impact of nuclear effects on $J/\psi$ meson production in proton-proton and lead-lead collisions at the LHC is investigated. A simple model of nuclear interactions is used, where the dipole cross section is represented through different optical models, thereby determining and comparing the impact of nuclear effects in pp scattering. In pPb collisions, the model also aligns with data from the LHC's minimum bias and jet-related measurements. Additionally, the model's predictions concerning J/$\psi$ nuclear broadening and suppression in PbPb collisions are made. It is notably found that using a dipole optical model alone is sufficient to explain observations of nuclear effects in high-energy nucleus-nucleus collisions up to a mass number Z=82.

The quadratic equation $x^2+ax+b=0$ can be solved using the quadratic formula, but when a and b are both prime numbers, it's an interesting situation. This paper explores a special case where the equation's solutions involve the powers of 7, specifically examining when the equation can equal $7^{2n}$ or $7^{2n+1}$. By identifying suitable prime numbers a and b, and calculating their products modulo $7^{2n+1}$, the paper uncovers patterns and constraints, ultimately presenting some theoretical proofs related to the Seven Flawed Conjecture.

The study is a detailed analysis of a liquid jet entering a channel of another liquid at a 90-degree angle, with the aim of developing a simplified model for further research.  By watching the jet become broken up into droplets, we understand that certain areas of the jet move faster than the surrounding fluid, while entrained air affects the dynamics and causes the jet to become unstable.  Using a combination of observations and earlier studies, we pinpoint the key factors that influence the breaking of the jet and develop two new factors that must be considered when studying this phenomenon.  Consequently, we suggest a simplified model that accounts for both the flow of the jet and the fluid around it, with the aim of understanding the breaking of the jet in terms of the forces acting upon it.

The widespread adoption of Apple's Arm-based processors has led to the Arm Architecture Reference Manual becoming a de-facto standard for software developers, which we refer to as the 'Arm Manual'. The Arm Manual serves as the primary source for Arm's instruction set architecture, describing functions that various processing units within Arm devices must adhere to. Over time, the Arm Manual has evolved through updates to describe new processor capabilities and functionalities. We aimed to create a computerized representation of the Arm Manual to facilitate better understanding of its revisions, which we call the 'Arm Architecture Knowledge'. Our Arm Architecture Knowledge was developed using the ARM architecture description languages and semantics, which define how function implementations interact with each other. This computerized knowledge enables us to explain and analyze updates to the Arm Manual, which we apply to Arm-based processors to ensure consistency in their functionality. We utilized the Arm Architecture Knowledge to examine variation in RISC-like processors, including those from Intel and Microchip, which we found to differ significantly from the Arm devices. Our Arm Architecture Knowledge effectively implements memory management with non-volatile memory, including the fundamental assumption that a single processor is executing, making it suitable for a wide range of applications. The Arm Architecture Knowledge, which is based on public documentation, does not rely on proprietary information and can be employed within open-source projects to develop innovative solutions for Arm devices.

This research presents a novel information network analysis framework called Hierarchical Document Topic Model (HDTM), enabling the assessment of multiple variables on a common scale. In contrast to conventional statistical approaches that consider individual variables in isolation, HDTM treats them as interconnected components of a comprehensive model. The efficacy of HDTM was demonstrated through simulations involving three different types of networks: academic publication co-authorship, social media post connectivity, and biomedical co-word occurrences. The outcome revealed that HDTM successfully identifies effective variables, whereas a widely-used alternative, the Lasso method, frequently overlooks significant variables. The analysis also uncovered variable interactions and hierarchies, and revealed a correlation between a variable's influence and its effectiveness. The study further examines the implications of masking variables on the model's accuracy and assesses the robustness of the results against network corruption. Overall, HDTM offers a versatile and efficient tool for exploring complex information networks.

A comprehensive examination, involving approximately 92,000 simulated three-body systems, was conducted to analyze their escape properties in a planar setting with one weakly bound particle surrounded by two more strongly bound particles. These systems were tracked over time until they either escaped or underwent a binary merger. Data collection spanned a vast range of masses, from equal to extremely disparate. Two distinct regimes were identified, based on the mass ratio: systems with a mass ratio greater than 1000 exhibited distinct, two-tiered escape characteristics, similar to theoretical predictions, whereas systems with lower mass ratios showed correlations between energy and angular momentum in their final configurations. Notably, the most energetic escapes were found to occur at specific, high eccentricity values. These findings are comparable to a recent study employing a distinct three-body system topology, with some notable differences.

The nuclear modification factor of prompt $\psi(2S)$ mesons in Au+Au collisions at $sqrt{s_{_{NN}}}=200$ GeV was measured. The data exclude a simple nuclear modification factor and exhibit a clear distinction from J/$\psi$ measurements within the same dataset. The ratio of $\psi(2S)$ to J/$\psi$ nuclear modification factors was found, and the data indicate the presence of different nuclear modification effects affecting the two states. The analysis accounted for potential sources of uncertainty related to prompt production assumptions and the determination of nuclear modification factors for $p+p$ collisions.

In a specific mathematical system called continuous logic, for any given complete metric space, we can define a novel equivalence relation. Furthermore, we establish that the quotient space obtained by dividing the space by this equivalence relation preserves key properties and is essentially equivalent to the original space. Additionally, we demonstrate the existence of a universal model with a specific property and show it satisfies a particular theorem.

Over time, large-scale software systems tend to lose continuity in their evolution, resulting in difficulties for developers to track down past changes. Our approach, involving the application of singular value decomposition, allows us to identify temporal patterns in software evolution by discovering underlying components of a software system's source code files, regardless of the time period in which they were modified. By focusing on the significant variations in software evolution, developers can target specific areas for improvement to achieve greater efficacy.

Recent advancements in deep sequential models have led to significant gains in accessibility and usability of self-supervised learning for structured data. Nevertheless, these models often struggle with sequences exceeding the maximum sequence length limit, a common issue with accessible deep self-supervised learning. To address this limitation, our research introduces an attention-based transfer learning approach, specifically for natural language, where a pre-trained model's weights are used to create multiple attention masks. These attention masks, generated based on input, output, and hidden state projections, enhance the capture of critical sequence information. Our experiments, conducted across six benchmark datasets covering various sequence lengths, demonstrate that this approach surpasses prior methods without this capability. Additionally, we developed and open-sourced the code for this technique, which is now available on GitHub at https://github.com/alecaxford/Deep-Seq-A2T.

A comprehensive examination of the complex magnetic field on the symmetric blast wave of Cassiopeia A, a supernova remnant, has been conducted across multiple wavelengths. The precise alignment of the magnetic field observed in X-ray and radio spectra suggests they share the same polarization angle, approximately 27 degrees. This alignment challenge existing models of shock dynamics is particularly pronounced in regions of the remnant's eastern edge where the field is particularly strong. The presence of intensely aligned magnetic fields, observed in multiple areas of the remnant, cannot be explained by simplified models of the explosion's initial dynamics, leading researchers to speculate that the fields may have played a significant role in shaping the explosion's symmetry.

The Basic Subset Sum Problem involves determining if there are distinct subsets, each no larger than a given size, whose combined sums equal specific values. This problem has applications in document classification, feature selection, and distributed computing, and it's considered an NP-complete problem. To address this, a new parameterized version of the problem was proposed, where the focus is on finding distinct subsets of a specific size containing unique elements. This variant was further studied by tightening the bounds on the complexity of solving it efficiently. This was achieved by establishing a connection between the problem and a new variant of the Clique problem, parameterized by the size of one of the vertices. This discovery led to an improvement in the known bounds on the complexity of solving this variant of the Subset Sum problem efficiently.

This study explores the quark core of compact stars, specifically stars that experience a deconfinement phase transition with two breaking points in their symmetries, denoted as $T_{\rm dc}^*$ and $T_{\rm dc}^{*2}$. We examine how this phase transition affects matter across diverse temperature and density conditions. The study also delves into the quark star configurations, taking into account both normal and superconducting quark states. It's noteworthy that superconducting quark stars have smaller radii compared to their normal quark counterparts. Additionally, we have determined the mass and radius relationships for hybrid stars containing neutron stars and various quark core components. These relationships indicate significant discrepancies based on the quark core model employed. Notably, hybrid stars containing two core components fall within the 1.2 to 2.0 solar mass range.

The performance of a gyroscopic system known as the compass state, which is optimized for measuring rotation around a singular axis, is examined. Optimization is achieved through a control-theoretic approach employing a nonlinear feedback loop to adjust a system variable called the anisotropy. As this adjustment is done in a real-world setting, imperfect precision is factored in, allowing a solution that balances performance and variability. This variation is reduced by solving a related stochastic problem that identifies the optimal point of balance between the compass state's properties and the limitations of real-world implementation. Specifically, the solution involves finding the best amount of anisotropy that can be introduced, which is a trade-off between being as sensitive as possible and being easily variable enough to accurately measure its own properties. This solution is then tested in a simulation that includes random errors, which validates the assumptions made and suggests improvements to the system's optimization.

Our method introduces a novel way to analyze single droplet breaks apart into smaller droplets, focusing on ejection dynamics. This process involves two key components: measuring the droplet's cross-sectional shape to determine if it's a traditional or distorted jet, and tracking the droplet's tip to identify the source of any instability that causes it to break. This method is utilized in studying the instability of liquid follicles and can be applied to other droplets under the influence of internal pressures.

Inspired by the self-organization of biological systems, we're examining a novel model of viral behavior where the interaction between the virus and host cell is driven by a physical transformation of the virus's surface. This model builds on an idea from molecular biology called viral surface metabolism, where the attachment of the virus to a host cell triggers a chemical reaction that reconfigures the virus's exterior. This change in the virus's surface modifies its interaction with other cells, enabling the virus to navigate to its target by responding to cellular signals, rather than relying on random motion. By simulating this process, we've observed the emergence of viral-like behavior in our model, where the simulated viruses exhibit directed movement towards mock host cells. This model offers a possible explanation for the virus's ability to navigate across cellular membranes without the need for complex navigation mechanisms.

A thorough examination of nine S-type and nine U-type galaxies was carried out, utilizing detailed data from spitzer and fake observations. The research revealed that galaxies of both types experience their disks warped at a distance of roughly 0.5-1.5 times the stellar bar length. However, the environment's impact differs significantly between S and U types. The warping of S-type galaxies is primarily induced by the nearby galaxy satellite, M81 M87. Contrarily, U-type galaxies have their disks mostly warmed by the central bar or the galaxy's central black hole. Moreover, it is observed that both types of galaxies are found in a variety of environments. The distinction that set S-type and U-type galaxies apart, the disk asymmetry, is also observed in both types. The research reveals that both types of galaxies are found in a variety of environments. The findings of the study suggest that both types of galaxies are capable of adapting to their surroundings. The environmental influence is thought to play a crucial role in shaping the distinct features of S and U-type galaxies.

This paper employs Yan's theorem on growth of harmonic functions to establish a dimension-based bound for gradient-shrinking Ricci solitons. Specifically, we demonstrate that if a complete gradient-shrinking Ricci soliton satisfies a certain growth condition, then it must have a dimension less than or equal to eight, provided it meets a specific volume condition. Furthermore, we prove the existence of a function with controlled growth on compact gradient-shrinking Ricci solitons, derived from Yan's original result.

Advanced quantum simulation techniques are essential for understanding the intricacies of complex materials physics. We've leveraged a density functional theory-based cluster perturbation theory to study the impact of electron-electron interactions in four-atom compounds of A$_2$B$_4$ type, where A is a alkali metal and B is a bismuthine. Our calculations accurately predicted the phase diagrams of KRbBi$_4$ and RbCsBi$_4$ and demonstrated that modest doping could modify the materials' structural symmetry and stability. We've observed the emergence of a superconducting state in both compounds under certain conditions, with RbCsBi$_4$ showing a $c$-axis-oriented unconventional superconductivity. Our findings suggest that these materials could potentially be used in topological superconducting quantum devices.

The response of dielectric boundaries is studied through the use of first-principles calculations, focusing on the non-adiabatic Born effective charges. It is observed that non-adiabatic charges arise from the interaction of electrons with long-wavelength longitudinal optical phonons, and are contingent on electronic boundary conditions. In cases where electronic boundary conditions are not satisfied, non-adiabatic charges are generated, and their behavior differs significantly between clean conductors and insulators. Furthermore, non-adiabatic charges result in the scattering of electrons by phonons, and can lead to electron heating and charge build-up at boundaries. In insulators, non-adiabatic charges are equivalent to those in doped insulators, and are maximized when boundary conditions are not met. In contrast, non-adiabatic charges in clean conductors are minimized. A quantitative comparison between clean conductors, doped insulators, and boundaries made of HfO$_2$/SiO$_2$/HfO, reveals that non-adiabatic charges in boundaries are approximately $10^{-2}$ times those in doped insulators, and are also dependent on the specific atomic species involved.

A comparison between the fluctuating hydrodynamics (FHD) and Navier-Stokes equations (NSE) has been established through an analytical framework. This comparison reveals that the NSE can replicate the statistical properties of a hydrodynamical system modeled by FHD, provided it incorporates an appropriate random forcing term. Furthermore, our analysis shows that the dissipation rate in both the FHD and NSE systems exhibits similar power-law behavior with respect to the wavenumber, yet the NSE systematically overestimates the dissipation rate by a factor of $\sqrt{2}$. This discrepancy emphasizes the role of random fluctuations in turbulent flows and underscores the limitations of the deterministic NSE in capturing the inherent randomness of turbulent fluid dynamics.

The Witten effect states that in a magneto-electric system, the presence of a quantum Hall effect inherently introduces an imbalance in charge and spin. Mathematically, this can be represented as an inverse Higgs mechanism, which in turn creates a type of boundary magnetoelectric coupling. Building upon this concept, we propose that the same underlying mechanism that causes the Witten effect can also give rise to an electric dipole moment in heavy ions when they are in the ground state. This theory provides an experimental approach to test the concept of multipoles in heavy ions. Additionally, we have discovered that the effective magnetic field produced by the dipole moment within the Dirac equation is precisely equivalent to the Goudsmit-Sakata rule, which describes the total orbital and spin magnetic moment of the last filled electron in an atom. This suggests a deeper connection between multipole moments, quantum numbers, and relativistic wave functions, which can be further explored in this study.

We're investigating an advanced statistical method called Diffusion-Approximate Time-Space (DATS) that makes predictions possible in highly complex problems. In this study, we apply DATS to a sophisticated system known as the Arnol'd-Hipparchus model, which is not easily solvable. By leveraging temporal and spatial data, DATS enables us to estimate the diffusion coefficient of the system, which significantly expands its effective dimensionality. We observe that increasing the delay in this system has a major impact on diffusion and the system's effective dimensionality. This finding confirms our preliminary hypothesis and demonstrates that DATS can analyze nonlinearity systems with significant time delays.

This paper presents a denotational interpretation of higher-order probabilistic programs that aligns with a standard operational semantics, filling a gap in a prior existing framework. In contrast to operational semantics, the denotational approach considers the program's structure from start to finish. To formalize non-interruptive programs with reference to external contexts, a new concept called stochastic graphs is introduced. Stochastic graphs facilitate the development of a stochastic evaluation graph for each program, which serves as a counterexample generator and a validator for the program's correctness. By deriving a final stochastic graph at the end of the program execution, the denotational method achieves a precise matching with operational semantics. The presented framework supports a probabilistic lambda-calculus with recursive functions, but excludes dynamic memory management, which is known to cause issues in both operational and denotational interpretations.

This paper focuses on improving design efficiency through mining, specifically conclusion stability and cross-project relevance. We have developed an approach that involves generating and refining conclusions in both practical and theoretical senses. Firstly, we utilize a Conclusive Designer to produce a stable conclusion by minimizing modifications to existing designs. Secondly, we established a predictive model based on the similarities between design objectives and conclusion formulas. Our results reveal that this method enhances conclusion stability and achieves greater generalization across projects than the current predictive model alone.

In this research, we investigate a de Sitter universe that arises from the interaction between a perfect fluid's non-relativistic matter and a holographic dark energy (HDE) situated at the cosmological de Sitter horizon. By leveraging the generalized HDE model introduced by Wei and Su, we derive the de Sitter vacuum expectation value of the energy-momentum tensor, $\langle \Theta^\mu _\nu \rangle$, which corresponds to negative pressure dark vacuum energy. We also observe that the future cosmological de Sitter horizon can be described as the solution to a complex Klein-Gordon field equation resulting from the field's time-dependent mass from the time-dependent HDE.

The concept of optimal orientations or directions plays a significant role in various optimization challenges. This concept can be formalized using sets of directions that are optimal for specific tasks, which are often found to be smooth and manifold-based. Exploiting this geometric property can significantly accelerate the convergence of optimization algorithms. This research delves into two related areas: (1) how to effectively leverage this optimization directionality, and (2) how to enhance the convergence speed of optimization algorithms by harnessing this smoothness property. To address the first question, a novel approach reformulates the optimization problem by directly incorporating the optimal directionality, resulting in a more resilient optimization solution. To answer the second question, a new gradient-based method and a more efficient quasi-Newton method have been created that take into account the optimal directionality for optimal performance.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring with identity. We define a prime ideal $I$ in $R$ as $1$-absorbing if $^{*}I^{*} \subseteq I$ for all subsets $I^{*}$ of $R$ where $I^{*} \supseteq I$. In this research, we classify prime ideals in ring $k_{N}[x]$ as $1$-absorbing according to specific conditions and examine the properties of the power of such ideals. Additionally, this study introduces a new concept of weakly $1$-absorbing prime ideals and investigates the characteristics of these ideals, specifically that the cube of a weakly $1$-absorbing prime ideal which is not a $1$-absorbing prime ideal must lie within a maximal ideal of $k_{N}[x]$.

A comparative study of four theoretical methods for calculating the way particles interact in the Standard Model's framework, specifically how the sigma mesons interact with other particles, has shown that their predictions for how these mesons decay into other particles agree well with each other. However, a recent calculation using the Ratzinger approach found that certain decay patterns for these mesons are more likely to occur than previously thought. Analysis of two particular decay patterns involving a particle called the rho meson revealed a small discrepancy, on the order of a few standard deviations, when compared to current experimental data, and suggested that new, beyond-the-SM physics might be involved. A subsequent study involving another particle, the omega meson, did not yield such discrepancies. A subsequent study involving a different theoretical approach and the same rho meson decay pattern found agreement with experimental data, and reduced the small discrepancy previously found to virtually zero.

The evaluation of cosmic web formation through pixel-level data is done by analyzing the relationship between density fluctuations and galaxy distributions. This study introduces a computational method to efficiently calculate the statistical relationships between adjacent pixels in a map of mass or galaxy density. The proposed technique yields accurate results within a reasonable computation time, allowing for a comprehensive examination of pixel pairs across varying distances. The correlation patterns observed in the two-dimensional plots of lag times reflect the underlying developmental stages of cosmic structures. Specifically, a prominent correlation with positive delays indicates the time gap between a mass overdensity peak and a galaxy count peak. The predicted relationship between lag times and correlation values is empirically validated. Moreover, the study demonstrates that more sophisticated models generate greater and more complex correlations.

In recent years, there has been significant growth in relational machine learning applications, particularly in pharmacology where compound-protein interactions are analyzed. To assess the reliability of these models, it is crucial to develop robust evaluation techniques that can identify whether certain pharmacological processes are logically possible. To address this need, we propose introducing a basic level of semantic restraint into model evaluation. This involves employing logical formulas that reflect the semantically implausible nature of certain relationships between compounds and proteins. Through our investigation of the generated datasets and models, we demonstrate the importance of incorporating this type of restraint for accurate learning, particularly in scenarios where background knowledge is limited. Our analysis further suggests the potential for logical formulas to serve as a benchmark for measuring model performance and as a guiding force in enhancing learning algorithms.

In developed nations, the monitoring of road conditions is often efficient and reliable due to conventional infrastructure, however, in many underdeveloped countries, the process is hindered by a lack of resources. To overcome this issue, a smartphone-based approach has been gaining attention. While existing solutions typically require users to manually select specific images for evaluation, which can be impractical in actual field settings. To tackle this problem, this research proposes an integrated system that automatically gathers relevant images from a user's drive, categorizes and preprocesses them for analysis, and then presents the processed data for evaluation. The system's performance was tested on a dataset collected from drives on over 212 roads in Mexico, where it demonstrated the ability to detect road conditions with 88% accuracy without the need for additional supervision.

Learning from expert demonstrations without an agent-sized environment is
practical, but comparing expert and agent actions in detail is
impossible, which hinders imitation learning. Our research reveals that
even small differences between environments can significantly impact the
imitation learning process, causing agents to misinterpret their
surroundings. To bridge this gap, we develop an innovative method that
uses an unsupervised learning technique to bridge the disparity between
environments, specifically by utilizing the irregularities in the expert's
policy. Our solution was tested on various tasks and was found to enable
imitation learning when direct evaluation is impossible.

We developed a computational model for protostar formation that accounts for the complex dynamics of a rapidly accretion gas cloud. Our model, based on a novel algorithm and precise mathematical equations, accurately solves the interactions between the protostar and the surrounding gas across various spatial and temporal scales. It takes into account the conservation of angular momentum, the viscoelastic behavior of the gas, and the protostar's effect on the gas through its gravitational interaction. As the model runs, it computes the gas cloud's collapse, protostar growth, and gas disk formation. Interestingly, our model indicates that high-angular momentum gas clouds may undergo fragmentation and form multiple stars, whereas low-angular momentum gas clouds will typically give rise to a single-star system. We've applied our model to various gas cloud configurations and are using it to investigate the influence of magnetic fields and other factors on the protostar formation process.

The task involves generating a compact representation of association rule learning outcomes using binary data. This can be achieved by representing the redundancy among association rules using a established formalism called associative tables, which are then subject to reduction through removal of irrelevant elements to minimize size. A method is proposed to discard rules that have no logical consequence, then discard those with negligible consequences using a measure called item confidence. The resulting compact representation comprises non-consequential association rules whose supports and item confidence values are below certain threshold values. These threshold values are determined using predictive information and optimal parameters are found using a metric called growth of description with pruning. The efficiency of the proposed method is evaluated using benchmark datasets and the compact representations are compared against traditional approaches in terms of size and time required to obtain them. The results indicate the proposed method yields significantly smaller representations and reduces processing time significantly compared to conventional approaches.

Our research delves into the relationship between mental health and crime, leveraging a unique, de-identified mental health dataset in conjunction with crime data from New York City. By utilizing statistical methods aimed at establishing causal links, we identify a notable correlation between receiving mental health treatment and a subsequent decrease in violent and property crime recidivism. Furthermore, our results reveal that individuals convicted of less serious offenses respond better to mental health treatment, with notable reductions also observed in those with a history of violence. We recognize the limitations of our findings, attributing them to the reliance on observational data rather than truly randomized experiments. Nonetheless, our analysis provides valuable insights into the effects of mental health treatment on criminal behavior.

This paper introduces a method to derive the generating functions of specific polynomial classes by dividing the generating functions of higher degree polynomials tailored to $(p,q)$-integral bases. Following this, we use the newly formed generating functions to examine key properties of these special polynomials.

Creating an accurate map of radio signal strength and quality is crucial for various wireless communication systems to operate in an optimized state. One approach to generating these maps involves collecting radio signal measurements from various locations and using them to create a map of signal strength and quality. However, measuring signal strength and quality requires significant resources to collect enough data, particularly in areas with low population density or where it is hard to access. To resolve this issue, we propose an efficient method for measuring signal strength and quality by identifying and optimizing the most useful locations to collect data. This method uses a measure of map uncertainty to guide the data collection process and can be used with different optimization techniques to find the best solution. We tested this method in different scenarios and compared it with existing methods that either collect data from all locations at once or from one location at a time, without considering the most useful locations. Our results show that the proposed method takes less time to create an accurate map and saves more data collection resources compared to these existing methods.

Anomaly detection in system management is crucial, but difficult with labeled data due to the cost and effort involved in identifying genuine anomalies. Therefore, an unsupervised method for detecting anomalies without requiring data labels is highly desirable. One approach to this problem is the use of one-class autoencoders, but their effectiveness depends on the quality of the data and can be easily tricked by synthetic data generated with little effort. In this research, a new method called PureFit is presented, using an evolutionary algorithm to optimize the one-class autoencoder and improve its robustness and accuracy in detecting anomalies by preventing the model from learning synthetic data and improving its robustness against noisy data. The evaluation of the PureFit method on various systems demonstrated its ability to improve anomaly detection and enhance robustness compared to existing methods.

We designed and conducted a unique evaluation, comparing multiple verification systems for neural machine translation. Typically, verification systems are tested in a controlled environment with a limited number of errors, but we wanted to see how they perform when dealing with the varied levels of noise that occur in real-world scenarios. We collected a large dataset of fact-checking examples, which included multiple levels of related facts, varying degrees of association with the statement, and the possibility of contradictory evidence. We tested six verification systems and observed significant differences in their performance under both clean and noisy conditions. Notably, we found that there was a correlation between performance and error levels, with scores improving as the amount of error decreased. We hope this unique evaluation and associated dataset will help researchers to better assess verification systems in practical scenarios.

Text data augmentation is a widely recognized technique that enhances model performance by transforming input data into new samples. While its effectiveness has been established in scenarios where dataset size can be increased through, for example, collecting more reviews or generating new text based on existing data, its value in resource-constrained environments with fixed training datasets is less clear. Our research aims to clarify this issue by examining whether augmenting the standard MNIST and CIFAR10 datasets improves accuracy and how various augmentation methods impact results. Our findings indicate that dataset augmentation is most beneficial when the original training dataset is large but sufficiently increases accuracy when the dataset is modest in size. Crucially, we identify that augmenting the dataset changes the effective dimension of the problem, creating opportunities for improvement, and presents a scalable solution for addressing the limitations of resource-constrained machine learning in deep learning.

This research investigates how a measure of weak convergence, denoted as $v_n\to v$, is utilized to estimate functions of model parameters. We consider a statistical model, whose parameters belong to a finite set $\Theta$. Each parameter value leads to a unique probability distribution $P_\xi$ and a corresponding sample average $T_n$. We aim to examine how the weak convergence of $v_n\to v$ is related to estimating functions of $\xi$. We demonstrate that the weak convergence $v_n\to v$ is equivalent to the statement that $\mathrm{E}_\xi[T_n(f)]\to \mathrm{E}_\xi[f(\xi)]$ for all continuous functions $f$. We also discuss a particular case of estimating a parameter $\xi$ that takes values in a group and show a unique representation theorem for central groups. We apply this result to solve the estimation of a rotation parameter in a torus-based model.

This research explores the concept of record linkage as a means to enhance data efficiency but also poses a risk of compromising individual privacy.
